33
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Activity sheet – Egyptian society
The noble class
In Egypt, people had different lifestyles according to the amount of wealth they had, just 
like people do today. The most privileged (fortunate) class in society was made up of 
people we call nobles. A person could be considered a noble for a number of reasons.
+ 1     How would the lifestyle of a vizier differ from the life of a slave? Write a short 
paragraph about the differences in the following things: 
 
 
•   their work 
  •   their clothing 
    •   their family life.
 
 
•  their homes   •   their leisure activities      
I hold an important 
position in the pharaoh’s 
government. I am a vizier, 
which is similar to the role 
of prime minister.
I am the pharaoh’s first cousin.  
I wear fine clothing and jewellery and my 
husband and I have already had expensive 
tombs made for when we die. Servants cook, 
clean, bring us trays of food and do all  
the housework.
I was lucky enough to be born  
into a wealthy noble family. Because my  
parents are nobles, I am too. I live with my family 
in a lovely home that is richly decorated and well 
furnished. Our house has a beautiful garden  
and a swimming pool with lotus flowers  
floating on the water.
I am a highly  
honoured military 
leader – commander in 
chief of the pharaoh’s 
army. As a noble man,  
I enjoy more privileges 
than many other  
people in Egypt.

Women
+ 1  Complete the following passage using the words in the box below.
 
 
Egyptian law gave women a number of important rights.  
 
A woman had the right to:
 
●own land in her own _______
 
●receive an _____________ from her father
 
●leave this inheritance to any person of her _______
 
●divorce her __________ under certain circumstances 
 
●__________ of her children if there was a divorce or separation
 
● support __________ from the children’s father after a divorce  
or separation.
 
2    As a general rule, women could not hold a position in government. Interestingly,  
one Egyptian woman actually ruled Egypt as pharaoh. Use the clues below to  
find out her name. 
_  _  _  _  _  _  _  _  _  _
 
●The first three letters spell something you wear on your head beginning with ‘h’.
 
●The next four letters are spelt like the word ‘sheep’, but with only one ‘e’.
 
● The last three letters spell a word that sounds like ‘soot’ but has a ‘u’ instead of  
two ‘o’s.
 
 This female ruler wore a false beard as a symbol, and presented herself as pharaoh.  
They accepted her as their ruler, and she built up a powerful trading empire, which 
greatly increased Egypt’s wealth. But to do this, she had to take the throne by force  
from her stepson, Thutmose III. When he grew older, Thutmose may have had his 
stepmother murdered. He then removed every trace of her name from monuments  
and other written records. But he could not remove her memory completely.
+ 3     Why do you think Thutmose wanted to erase the people’s memories of his

Activity sheet – Egyptian society
Slaves
Some people in Egypt were served by slaves. Historians are not sure whether these 
workers were forced into slavery, or whether they were low-paid servants. It seems that 
slaves in Egypt were not considered to be the ‘property’ of a master. Rather, they were 
employed to perform certain duties that wealthier people did not wish to do. 
Activities of slaves
The activities of slaves included watering, planting and harvesting crops, cleaning the 
house, chopping firewood, moving cows to new grazing areas, feeding goats and pet cats 
and dogs, and moving bricks, timber and equipment for use in building projects.
+ 1   Summarise this information by finding some examples from the paragraph above 
to fill these spaces:

●household jobs, like ________________________  and  ______________________.
 
●caring for animals, such as ______________________ and ___________________.
 
●transporting materials and products. For example, ____________________________.
Sometimes people became slaves because they had a debt that they could not afford to 
repay. Others were prisoners of war, or had committed a crime that required punishment. 
If your parents were slaves, usually you would become a slave too.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Egypt 1
40
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Activity sheet – Daily life in Ancient Egypt
Food and drink 
+ 1   In the following text, circle all the words that name meats, vegetables, herbs 
and spices.
2 Draw squares around all the words that name fruits.
3 Underline all the other foods and drinks that are mentioned.
 
● Ancient Egyptian people ate a simple diet of vegetables, fruits, dairy products, 
eggs, meat and fish. They ate salad vegetables, including cucumber, lettuce 
and radishes, and cooked vegetables, including beans, peas, cabbage, leeks, 
onions and garlic. They also used corn, chickpeas, olive oil, bak tree oil and salt. 
 
● They grew emmer (a type of wheat) and barley – these grains were ground 
into flour for making flat bread and barley cakes. 
 
● Food was roasted, fried, boiled, baked, grilled or stewed. Spices and 
condiments included mustard, cumin, dill, coriander, cinnamon, rosemary, 
wild marjoram and vinegar. 
 
● Food was prepared on the floor or on low tables and was cooked, served and 
stored in clay dishes. Among the wealthy, gold, silver and bronze dishes, pots 
and cups were used.
 
●The wealthy ate much better diets than the poor and working classes. 
 
● Fruits that grew in Egypt included pomegranates, figs, melons, dates and grapes.
 
● Meat was eaten only occasionally, and included lamb, goat, hare and duck. 
Fish was more common, because of the Nile river. 
 
● Beer was made from fermented bread and wine was made from grapes. 
Milk and cheese were produced from the herds of cattle and goats the Ancient 
Egyptians kept. Eggs were harvested from wild birds, including ducks and geese. 
 
● Honey and palm sugar were readily available to sweeten foods. A sweet root 
called chuba, which grew near the Nile, was also used as a sweetener, and 
carob was used to add taste. Raisins were made from grapes and added to 
barley cakes to make sweet treats. 
 
● People generally ate with their fingertips. Bowls of scented water were used 
to wash fingers and hands when they became greasy.

42
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Daily life in Ancient Egypt
Egyptian clothing (1)
In Ancient Egypt, clothes were made of linen. This fabric was woven from the flax plant 
that the Egyptians farmed. It was usually white, but was sometimes dyed different colours. 
Noble men wore knee-length skirts and some also wore tunics. Men from the lower 
classes wore loincloths, which were much shorter. These enabled them to move about 
freely as they worked in the heat of the Egyptian sun.
Women wore long dresses and shawls.  
Both men and women wore cloaks in the cooler months. 
Royal and noble people sometimes wore animal skins 
over their shoulder. Everyone wore sandals made from 
flax or date palm fibre, and sometimes used leather to 
make their shoes last longer. Children mostly wore no 
clothes at all. 
Both men and women wore jewellery made of gold and silver, 
make-up on their faces, and elaborate wigs. For parties and other 
special occasions, people would dress up in their finest clothes. 
People would apply fragrant oils to their skin to make 
themselves smell nice, and some women wore wax cones filled 
with fragrance on their heads. As the lady became warmer 
throughout the event, the wax would melt, sending the fragrance 
trickling down their hair or wig, giving off a pleasant smell.
The Egyptians used different colours of 
ochre, mixed with oil or water, to make paints 
used in tomb paintings. Ochre was also used 
as make-up by both women and men. An oily, 
black eye make-up was used to help protect 
the eyes from the desert sand. It was made 
from an ochre called kohl.
Draw and colour this person’s face in 
Egyptian style make-up. Add some hair or  
a wig.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Egypt 1
48
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Activity sheet – Ancient Egyptian religion
The priesthood
Priests were very important members of Ancient Egyptian society. They supervised the 
running of temples, where ceremonies and rituals were carried out to honour the gods 
and goddesses. The priests employed at temples decided who could visit and answered 
people’s questions about the gods through a system of offerings. They would charge 
people money to have prayers offered, and accepted food and other objects as offerings 
to the gods. This filled up the temples with huge reserves of gold, silver, precious stones 
and other valuable objects. As a result, the priesthood grew wealthy and powerful. 
In the New Kingdom (around 1350 BCE), the priests of Amun had more power than the 
pharaoh himself. This prompted the pharaoh Akhenaten to declare that everyone stop 
worshipping all other gods except his own.
Temples were built to stand the test of time. They were made of huge columns, hand-
carved from sandstone, limestone and granite. Many of these colossal structures, such  
as the temple of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahri, are still standing today.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Egypt 1
51
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Death and funerary customs
Tombs
Pyramids were massive triangular-shaped buildings 
that were the tombs of the pharaohs. Historians 
know quite a lot about how the Ancient Egyptians 
learnt the art of pyramid building, because they 
studied some of the failed attempts. When pyramid 
building became too expensive, the Egyptians used 
tombs cut into the rocks at places such as the Valley of the Kings.
Early tombs
The earliest tombs were simple sandpits dug in the desert. Before the Egyptians began 
making mummies, the bodies would quickly dry out because of the hot sand and sun. 
Later, rectangular coverings called mastabas were built over the top of sandpits to mark 
and protect the graves.
Building pyramids
In later times, people began building tombs that were made of one mastaba on top of 
another, each one slightly smaller. This formed a step pyramid, like the one found at 
Saqqara. Early attempts to create a triangular-shaped pyramid failed because of mistakes 
in measurements. One attempt created the Bent Pyramid. It has a rounded top and 
unevenly sloping sides.
A true pyramid
Eventually, the Ancient Egyptians perfected pyramid building, to create the Great Pyramid 
of Khufu and many other pyramids throughout Egypt.
+  1   Draw a flowchart showing the development of tomb building in your workbook.  
Use these labels and add pictures.
sandpit    
mastaba    
step pyramid   
bent pyramid 
a true pyramid
When pharaohs in the Old Kingdom built their 
pyramids, nobles scrambled for burial sites as close  
as possible to the structures. They believed that being 
buried near a god-king would help them to pass the 
judgment of the dead and enter the afterlife.
© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 92209 042 3

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Egypt 1
52
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Death and funerary customs
Preserving the dead
The Ancient Egyptians believed in a life after death that would go on forever. It was very 
important to the Egyptians that the body of a deceased person be preserved. They treated 
and wrapped dead bodies to make them last a long time. We call these bodies mummies, 
and the process of making them is called mummification.
The Egyptians believed that people had three aspects to their soul. In writing and 
paintings, they drew them like this:
the ba
The ba was the personality – it was unique to the individual, and 
could be compared to the idea of a person’s ‘spirit’. It could roam the 
earth during daylight hours while Re the sun god was shining, then 
had to return to the underworld at night. The ba flew away from the 
body when the person died. If it was to return to the body later, it would need to be able 
to find and recognise the right body.
the ka
The ka was the ‘life force’ of the person that is common to all living 
humans – the ‘breath’ that made them alive. The ka entered the body 
at birth and was the force that preserved life. It was the same for 
each person. It was believed that at death, the ka needed a body to 
use for its eternal home – hence the need for mummification. Ancient Egyptians knew 
that the original physical body of a person eventually decayed away, but they believed the 
ka needed the shell created by the cloth wrappings and the decorated coffin as a physical 
place it could return to eternally.
the akh
The third part of the soul, the akh, was believed to be the part that 
faced judgment for the person’s conduct while they were alive. The 
akh could only travel to the afterlife once judgment was complete. 
The Egyptians also mummified certain animals for ceremonial 
reasons. Many mummies of cats have been found in tombs, along 
with preserved crocodiles and birds. It is believed that the Egyptians wanted these 
animals to accompany them into the afterlife.

© Ally Chumley and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Warfare in Egypt
The warrior pharaohs
Egyptians were generally a peace-loving people. But the pharaoh needed to protect 
his nation from invaders. At various times, the Canaanites, the Assyrians, the Hittites, the 
Hyksos and the Mitanni all threatened to invade Egypt. 
Winning battles
Certain pharaohs, including Thutmose III and his son Amenhotep II, were successful in 
defeating their neighbours. These pharaohs battled their enemies, took some people 
captive, then made the defeated countries pay money and goods (tribute) to  
Egypt for many years.
Warrior pharaohs
Being a successful pharaoh wasn’t 
easy. The warrior pharaohs 
actually went into battle, leading 
their troops from the chariot 
at the very front of the ranks. It 
was a brave (or foolish) thing 
to wage war against an enemy, 
particularly one with a large army. 
But Thutmose III and Amenhotep 
II did so successfully, and were 
able to expand Egypt’s empire 
by winning battles on land and 
sometimes at sea.
Occasionally, a person born into a lower class in Egypt could rise up through 
the ranks of society because of their abilities as a soldier. This was achieved by a 
military general called Horemheb, who was the first person not born into royalty 
to become pharaoh. He achieved this high status because of his accomplishments 
as a military leader.

Conflict within Egypt
During one difficult period of Egyptian history, a foreign people called the Hyksos had 
come to live in the land. Historians once believed that the Hyksos had entered Egypt by 
staging a violent invasion. But more recent research suggests that they may have come 
peacefully at first, perhaps in small numbers, but soon grew to be a threat to the nation’s 
security and way of life. The Hyksos were from a region north-east of Egypt. A number of 
different pharaohs tried to remove them. It was King Ahmose who finally drove them out.

Egypt’s trading partners
The Ancient Egyptians traded to obtain goods that were not available in Egypt. Timber 
was in short supply, and was one of the main commodities (products) traded. The main 
commodity that Egypt’s neighbours wanted was food – grains such as wheat, corn and 
barley. These were Egypt’s main exports. An export is a commodity that is sent out of a 
country. Egypt also exported gold, linen, papyrus, glass, and sculptures and other objects 
made of stone.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Egypt 1
62
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Activity sheet – Foreign relations
Trading with the neighbours
Egypt didn’t only send out exports. The government also obtained essential items from 
neighbouring nations. Items that are brought into a country are called imports. Egypt 
imported these items from neighbouring countries.
Nubia 
gold
incense
slaves
Palestine
oil jugs 
pottery dishes 
Byblos 
timber
metals 
Punt 
monkeys 
baboons
leopard skins
perfumes
ebony
ivory
Greece
olive oil
wine
marble
 
 
Queen Hatshepsut built up trade between Egypt and neighbouring countries during 
her reign. Although she is remembered as one of the only female pharaohs, and for her 
dispute with her stepson Thutmose III, Hatshepsut made some important new trading 
relationships with Egypt’s neighbours.
+  Imagine you were an Egyptian trader. How much Egyptian grain would you pay for 
each of these commodities? Enter numbers to show how many sacks of grain you 
would trade.
1  two leopard skins 
  I would trade __________ 20 kilogram sacks of grain.
2  a tonne of cedar wood   I would trade __________ 20 kilogram sacks of grain.
3  twelve bottles of wine   I would trade __________ 20 kilogram sacks of grain.
+  How much Egyptian linen would be a fair exchange for each of the following?
4  100 litres of olive oil 
  I would trade __________ metres of linen fabric.
5  10 Nubian slaves 
  I would trade __________ metres of linen fabric.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Egypt 1
63
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Activity sheet – Foreign relations
Booty and tribute
When the Egyptian army defeated an enemy nation, the soldiers were ordered to find and 
take as much property as they could find. Anything that was taken from an enemy in a 
time of war was called booty.
Booty might include gold, silver, precious gemstones, jewellery, items made from ivory or 
other expensive materials, weapons, cloth, tents and chariots. Booty could also include 
slaves, captive citizens, horses, cattle and other animals.
When an enemy had been defeated in battle, the pharaoh made the people of that nation 
pay a special tax called tribute to the government of Egypt. Every year, the pharaoh would 
send his representatives to collect the tax. It was sometimes paid in the form of seed, grain 
from the harvest of crops, animals, equipment or other valuable items.
+  Read the text above and then complete the following sentences.
1  Booty is _________________________________________________________________ . 
2  Booty could include items such as _________________________________________
____________________________________. It could also include people and animals, 
such as ____________________________________.
3  Tribute is _______________________________________________________________ 
_________________________________________________________________________ . 
4  This could take the forms of ________________________________________________
_________________________________________________________________________ .
5  Tribute was collected by __________________________________________________
_________________________________________________________________________ .

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Egypt 1
64
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Activity sheet – Foreign relations
The first peace treaty
At the height of Egypt’s power, Rameses the Great signed the world’s first documented 
peace treaty. Rameses wanted to reach an agreement that would benefit both him and 
his enemies, the Hittites. This type of politics is called diplomacy. The Egyptians and the 
Hittites agreed:
 
●upon the exact borders and territories belonging to each country
 
●not to attack each other
 
●to help each other if either country was attacked
 
●to help each other in emergencies
 
●to give up any rebels or political prisoners hiding within their borders.
+ 1    Imagine you are Rameses the Great. Use your imagination to write a creative 
journal entry about the day you signed this treaty with the Hittite king. Explain 
why you are so happy about it.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
5
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Objectives
l To be able to recognise the main geographic 
features of Ancient Greece and find it on a 
world map
l To learn about the topography and climate of 
Ancient Greece 
l To discuss how the terrain and Mediterranean 
climate of Ancient Greece influenced farming 
practices and diet
Prior knowledge
Students should have some basic map-reading 
skills and be able to find their own country 
on a world map. They should also have a basic 
understanding of the relationship between climate 
and agriculture.
Background
Greece is located in a region known for its mild 
climate and proximity to trade routes. Its location 
influenced many aspects of Ancient Greek 
society. The diet of the Ancient Greeks was largely 
determined by the topography of the land, its 
closeness to open and sheltered seas, and the 
climate of the area. These factors also influenced 
modes of transport and popular activities. For 
example, the Ancient Greeks were strong seafarers – 
they used boats to trade, transport goods and fight 
wars. 
Starter activity
As a class, use an atlas to identify where Greece is. 
Tell students that Greece didn’t always have the 
same boundaries as the national borders that apply 
today. In fact, at times Ancient Greece was larger and 
included many different settlements. Discuss the 
sorts of factors that could have influenced how large 
Ancient Greece was – for example, wars, migration 
and trade. 
Also discuss what is meant by a polis. This is covered 
briefly in the first resource sheet, but extra discussion 
would help students understand the concept of 
independent states, with their own laws and systems of 
government.
Resource and Activity sheets
Have students read the information on the Resource 
sheet ‘Map of Ancient Greece’ and study the map. 
Discuss the information provided. Ensure that students 
understand what polis means. Help students to 
pronounce the names of different poleis. Students 
should then complete the Activity sheet ‘The land of 
Ancient Greece’, referring to the Resource sheet as 
required.
Have students read the two Resource sheets on 
‘Farming in a Mediterranean climate’. Discuss the way 
climate and topography influence farming. Also discuss 
the role of the sea in providing food. Have students 
work in pairs to complete the Activity sheet ‘Farming 
life’. They can write their answers in their workbooks if 
they need more space.
Extension activity
Ask the class to discuss the role of technology in 
farming practices and food transportation. Use the 
following questions as prompts for discussion: What 
types of food do you eat every day? Where does this 
food come from? Is it farmed locally or does it come 
from far away, perhaps even overseas? If so, how does 
it get here? Farmers and fishermen in Ancient Greece 
did not have access to modern technology – in what 
ways would the absence of modern technology have 
influenced what they farmed and the way they farmed 
it? How would they have transported their food and 
how does this differ to the way we transport our food?
Answers
The land of Ancient Greece  1 mountainous; 2 Miletus, 
Phacaea; 3 the Peloponnese; 4 Olympia; 5 True; 6 False;  
7 False; 8 True

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
11
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Origins of Ancient Greece
Objectives
l To learn about the origins of Ancient Greece
l To learn about three civilisations of Ancient 
Greece
l To explore the way geography shaped the 
development of the city-states of Athens  
and Sparta
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic understanding of the 
geography of Ancient Greece.
Background
Ancient Greece evolved over thousands of years. At 
different times during this period, different cultures 
dominated the region. Each cultural era promoted 
different ways of doing things, so that there were 
different practices and beliefs during each of the 
stages of Greek history. As centuries passed, cities 
were settled (or conquered) by ‘outsiders’, and 
(in many cases) they in turn were ‘invaded’. Three 
dominant civilisations of Ancient Greece were the 
Minoans, the Mycenaeans and the Dorians. 
Starter activity
If you have not already done so, give students a copy 
of the Resource sheet ‘Map of Ancient Greece’ from 
unit 1. Use it as the basis for a class discussion around 
the following questions: What was it about the 
topography of Ancient Greece that made land travel 
difficult? What might have been an easier way for 
the Ancient Greeks to get around? Do you think they 
would have been content to stay in one city for their 
whole lives? What reasons might people have had for 
venturing beyond their own polis (city-state)?
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet ‘The Bronze and Dark Ages’ 
introduces students to three dominant cultures of 
Ancient Greece: the Minoans, the Mycenaeans and the 
Dorians. Discuss the information provided with students 
and talk to them about what a civilisation is. Remind 
students of the way that years are counted BCE (‘Before 
the Common Era’), i.e. backwards from the Year 1 CE. 
before they complete Activity sheet ‘Through the ages’. 
The Resource sheets ‘Landscape and the 
development of Athens’ and ‘Landscape and the 
development of Sparta’ help students identify the 
distinctive geographical features of Athens and Sparta 
and encourage them to consider how these features 
influenced the development of these two important 
poleis. 
The Activity sheet ‘Barriers for expansion’ 
consolidates what students have learnt from the 
resource sheets. Students can work with a partner 
to complete it.
Extension activity
Discuss the impact of geography on the development 
of poleis throughout Ancient Greece. Compile a class list 
of the types of natural features that can limit movement 
between cities and the expansion of a civilisation (for 
example, mountains, seas, deserts etc). Ask students to 
consider whether such features limit social expansion 
and connection today in the same way that they did 
thousands of years ago. How have modern societies 
overcome geographical boundaries? Are there any 
disadvantages to some means such as motorised 
transport and the internet?
Answers
Through the ages  1 Peloponnese; 2 civilisation; 3 
bronze; 4 Minos; 5 Mycenaeans; 6 Dark; The Minoans 
settle in Crete – 2500 BCE; The Dorians invade – 1000 
BCE; The Mycenaeans conquer the Minoans – 1400 BCE.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
17
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Politics and governance
Objectives
l To understand what is meant by polis/poleis 
l To identify the features of different forms of 
government in Ancient Greece: aristocracies, 
dictatorships, oligarchies and democracies
l To learn about the rights of citizens (men), and 
to learn that non-citizens (women, slaves and 
foreigners) had no political rights
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities.
Background
Ancient Greece operated as a unified nation only 
during times of war or mass celebration. As a result, 
forms of governance varied between poleis (city-
states). The four dominant forms of governance in 
Ancient Greece were aristocracies, dictatorships, 
oligarchies and democracies.
Starter activity
Write the word governance on the board. Ask 
students to brainstorm what they associate with 
governance. Write all suggestions on the board. Then 
write the following definition on the board and ask 
students to copy it into their books:
Governance refers to a system used to manage a 
community, organisation or nation.
Explain that in Ancient Greece there were 
many forms of governance and that these differed 
between poleis. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet ‘Governing the poleis’ introduces 
students to the four dominant forms of governance 
discussed in this unit, as well as some of the inequalities 
in Ancient Greek society. 
The Activity sheet ‘Leadership and rights’ first 
asks students to recap what they have learnt, then 
asks students to consider who they think would 
make a better ruler, an aristocrat or a tyrant. Discuss 
this question with the class. Mention that in Ancient 
Greek times the word tyrant did not have the negative 
connotations we now associate with it, and that often 
the people supported a tyrant. Finally, students are set 
some discussion questions about rights.
The Resource sheets ‘Spartan oligarchy’ and ‘Athenian 
democracy’ can be worked through together as a class. 
It may be helpful to project the sheets onto a large 
screen so that students can follow the information both 
individually and collectively. Then have students form 
pairs to complete the Activity sheet ‘Who’s in charge?’, 
which helps them summarise what they have learnt.
Have students work in small groups to complete the 
Activity sheet ‘Voting rights’, then report their conclusions 
to the whole class. Note these on the board. Finally, 
summarise class findings and add any that have been 
missed. For example: all adults can vote, voting applies 
to all levels of government, elections are held regularly 
(every three to four years).
Extension activity
Athenian democracy was only one type of democracy. 
Other democratic poleis formed their own rules and 
democratic structures. As a class, ask students to create 
the structure of a democracy for their school. They 
can decide who can vote, what they can vote on, how 
often meetings take place and who can attend. Invite 
students to use their imaginations and not be limited  
by current rules and structures!
Answers
Leadership and rights 1 wealthy, noble families;  
2 a dictator or tyrant; 3 a dictator; 4 False; 5 False; 6 True

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
24
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Everyday life
Objectives
l To learn about the different social groups and 
strata that made up Ancient Greek society
l To recognise the differences between the way 
males and females lived and were treated in 
Ancient Greek society, including differences in 
education and everyday duties
l To understand the importance of presentation, 
grooming and exercise in Ancient Greek society
Prior knowledge
Students should know that Ancient Greece was 
made up of independent city-states called poleis. 
They should also have some understanding that 
Ancient Greek society was not equitable.
Background
Ancient Greek society was very different to 
contemporary Western society. It was ordered and 
hierarchical, slaves were integral, and females were 
considered socially and intellectually inferior to 
males. However, while life in Ancient Greece was 
very different to life today, many of the things we 
now take for granted, such as voting and education, 
had their origins in Ancient Greece. Grooming was 
an important part of everyday life in Ancient Greece, 
much as it is in our society today.
Starter activity
As a class, identify evidence of social structure 
in modern Western society. For example, do all 
children have to go to school? Are there differences 
between the jobs men and women can do? Do we 
have different ‘classes’ of people? Are some people 
prevented from owning land or voting? Then ask 
them how they think day to day life might have 
been different for people living in Ancient Greece.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet ‘Social strata’ presents students 
with a visual representation of the social structure of 
Athens and Sparta. Discuss the information provided. 
Ensure that students understand what strata means. 
Help students to pronounce the names of each social 
stratum. Discuss how people in higher strata had more 
rights and opportunities than those in lower strata. 
The Activity sheet ‘Social groups in Athens and 
Sparta’ is designed for students to summarise what they 
have learnt.
The Resource sheets ‘Family life in Athens’ and 
‘Family life in Sparta’ allow students to compare and 
contrast the life of an Athenian family with the life of 
a Spartan family. Students can then work in pairs to 
complete the Activity sheet ‘Life in Athens and Sparta’.  
You could then discuss their answers as a class and 
note them on the board. Similarities include the nuclear 
family unit and the fact that the father is the head of  
the family; differences include the focus on military 
life for Spartan males and the focus on fitness for both 
sexes in Sparta.
In the Activity sheet ‘Making a good impression’ 
students are presented with some opinions about the 
importance of grooming, presentation and physical 
activity in Ancient Greece. Students are encouraged to 
compare our current focus on physical appearance and 
exercise with that of the Ancient Greeks.
Extension activity
Ask the class: Was life in Ancient Greece easy or  
difficult? How different would it have been living in 
each social class? You could also compare and contrast 
the influence of modern technology on society:  
Modern technology is central to our lives today, but  
in Ancient Greece they did not have such technology. 
How different would it have been to live in Ancient 
Greece without technology? Consider both work and 
leisure activities.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
31
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Warfare
Objectives
l To learn about the role of the hoplites and the 
military strategy of the phalanx
l To understand the importance of the military in 
Ancient Greece, especially for the Spartans
l To recognise the role of the Ancient Greek fleet 
in sea-battles and learn about triremes
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic understanding of 
the geography of Ancient Greece. Students should 
also have completed unit 4, Everyday life, and/or 
have an appreciation of the role of the military in 
Spartan society.
Background
Ancient Greece was made up of separate poleis (city-
states) that only came together as a unified nation 
for significant ceremonies and events, and in times 
of war. The Ancient Greeks were considered to be 
worthy adversaries and had a reputation for being 
brave and intelligent warriors. This was especially 
evident in the loyalty shown by the hoplites and 
the development of military strategies such as the 
phalanx (foot soldier formation).
Sea-based warfare was also a staple of ancient 
battles in the Mediterranean, and the Greeks were 
considered masters of it. Their creation and mastery 
of the trireme, coupled with their bravery and fierce 
loyalty to Hellas (Greece), saw them win many 
conflicts against much larger fleets. 
Much of their fighting was internal, for example 
between Athenians and Spartans.
Starter activity
Ask students what, if anything, they have heard about 
Ancient Greek warfare. Have they, for instance, seen 
movies such as The 300 Spartans, or heard of the Battle 
of Marathon? Have they heard the terms hoplite or 
phalanx before, and do they know what they mean? Ask 
students how they think the Ancient Greeks might have 
fought against each other and foreign enemies? What 
sorts of weapons might they have used? Have students 
refer to the map of Ancient Greece from unit 1, and ask 
them to consider the role of the sea in Ancient Greek 
warfare.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet ‘The hoplites and the phalanx’ and 
the Activity sheet ‘Preparing for battle’ provide students 
with a comprehension activity. Read the Resource sheet 
as a class, discuss the information then have students 
complete the activity.
The Activity sheet ‘The Battle of Marathon’ includes 
activities that help students gain an understanding of 
the story of Pheidippides and the origins of the modern 
marathon.
Read the Resource sheet ‘The fleet’, then complete 
the Activity sheet ‘Triremes’. You could take the class out  
into the yard and measure out the size of a trireme to 
help students comprehend how small and crowded 
they were. 
Extension activity
Discuss how different warfare in Ancient Greece  
would have been compared to modern warfare. For 
example, hoplites had to walk to battlegrounds carrying 
their own armour and weapons, combat was face-to-
face and bloody; and sieges were a common way of 
undermining a city’s resilience. Is it surprising, then,  
that courage and fitness were emphasised so strongly 
in Ancient Greek culture?

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
37
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Religion
Objectives
l To understand the meaning of the word myth
l To recognise the significance of mythology to 
the Ancient Greeks
l To learn about the most important Titans and 
Olympian gods in Ancient Greek mythology 
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities.
Background
Ancient Greek mythology is one of the great 
hallmarks of the ancient world. Not only were the 
Ancient Greeks polytheists – that is, they believed 
in more than one god – but they also believed that 
their gods were acutely interested in the lives of 
humans. Ancient Greek mythology is a collection 
of stories featuring the various gods and often 
including heroes and humans as well.
Starter activity
Write the word myth on the board. Ask students 
to brainstorm everything they associate with 
myths. Write all suggestions on the board. Then ask 
students if they’ve heard any myths, or even parts 
of myths. Can they share them with the class? Can 
students name any of the Ancient Greek gods? 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet ‘Ancient Greek mythology’ 
introduces students to the main kinds of characters 
in Ancient Greek myths: Olympian gods, Titans, 
heroes and humans. The Activity sheet ‘The gods’ 
helps them consolidate what they have learnt and 
then read some background on one of the most 
important gods, Zeus. 
The Activity sheet ‘Athena and Arachne’ 
introduces a simple myth to students, with an 
accompanying cloze activity.
You could have students work in small groups to 
complete the Activity sheet ‘The myth of Demeter, 
Persephone and Hades’. After reading through the 
myth together, they could discuss their answers before 
writing their own responses in their workbooks. 
The final Activity sheet, ‘Mythology and everyday life’, 
summarises some aspects of Ancient Greek religious life, 
with a cloze activity.
Extension activity
All societies have their own creation myths – stories that 
explain how people came to exist, what their purpose in 
life is, and what the afterlife (if, according to a particular 
social group, it exists) looks like. Ask students to suggest 
reasons why creation myths evolve – for example, 
people prefer belief to uncertainty, myths support belief 
systems and help provide social order, myths/beliefs can 
be used to justify actions. Ancient Greek mythology also 
tends to be very patriotic, with male gods assuming the 
positions of most power and female gods tending to 
focus on home and children. Can students identify any 
examples? Responses could be written in two columns 
on the board (one listing ‘powerful’ gods and one listing 
‘kind’ gods) and students could be asked why they think 
there was a gender division.
Answers
The gods legendary, contest, ruler, scared, mad, disloyal
Athena and Arachne Arachne, please, bad, goddess, 
woman, weaving, weaving, arachnids
Mythology and everyday life gods, sea, weather, please, 
approve, ceremonies, statues, angered, punished, right, 
goddesses, children, god, Bible, community

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
43
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Art
Objectives
l To identify art forms (including theatre, 
sculpture, pottery and music) that were central 
to Ancient Greek society 
l To recognise the significance of art to the 
Ancient Greeks
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities.
Background
Art was very important to the Ancient Greeks.  
Their culture and beliefs were expressed through 
various art forms, including music, theatre, sculpture 
and painted pottery. The Ancient Greeks honoured 
the gods and their society through these art forms, 
and developed a very rich and varied artistic  
culture, examples of which still survive today and 
which still influence modern day artists, musicians 
and playwrights.
Starter activity
Write the word art on the board. Ask students what 
they think of when they hear or see the word art. 
Do they think only about paintings and drawings? 
Can they think of any other art forms? Prompt 
students, if required, to consider things such as 
sculpture, music and theatre as art also. Ask students 
if they can think of any examples of Ancient 
Greek art. Statues will often be the most common 
response. Invite students to share anything they 
already know about Ancient Greek art. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet ‘Theatre’ introduces students to the 
Greek theatrons by having them label a diagram. The 
final activity requires them to create a mask of their 
own. You may need to discuss this as a class first, to get 
students thinking about the ways they can design their 
masks to depict different emotions and characters. For 
example, female masks might have long hair, masks 
depicting old characters might have excessive wrinkles, 
and angry masks might have furrowed brows and hard, 
straight mouths. 
The Activity sheet ‘Sculpture’ contains information 
about this important aspect of Ancient Greek art. 
Students then answer questions about one of the 
statues presented. They can do this individually in their 
workbooks or through discussion in pairs.
The Activity sheet ‘Painted pottery’ provides 
information and then asks students to draw their  
own design. The sheet can be completed individually  
or in pairs.
The Activity sheet ‘Music’ introduces some Ancient 
Greek instruments. The questions can be answered 
individually or students could work in pairs to respond 
to them.
Extension activity
Art best comes to life when students can feel, experience, 
hear and build the various art forms discussed. To this 
end, the class could work on a play that depicts an 
aspect of Ancient Greek life or a Greek myth they have 
studied. Tasks could be divided between students 
and could include: play writing, costume design, mask 
making, acting, singing and music. This could be either 
an elaborate or a simple project, depending on the 
resources and time available.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
48
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Architecture
Objectives
l To recognise the main features of Ancient 
Greek buildings: angularity, columns and 
decorations
l To recognise the main differences between the 
Doric, Ionic and Corinthian styles
l To understand that Greek architecture evolved 
over time 
Prior knowledge
Students should have completed unit 1 (Land and 
sea) and unit 7 (Art) before commencing this unit. 
Background
Ancient Greek architecture was not only very 
distinctive and beautiful, but its style has influenced 
many architects throughout the ages. Like most 
civilisations, the architecture of the Ancient Greeks 
reflected not only their aesthetic values, but also their 
beliefs and the things they considered important. 
Mythology was extremely important to the Ancient 
Greeks, and this is evidenced by the extensive use of 
decorative elements such as friezes and statues, as 
well as by the fact that temples were among the most 
elaborate and impressive structures they built.
Starter activity
The built structures of a civilisation reveal a lot about 
the interests, beliefs, values and lifestyles of its people. 
Write the phrase ‘What do our buildings say about us?’ 
on the board. Invite students to think about what our 
buildings reveal about their contemporary culture. 
For example, which are the largest buildings in our 
society? Which buildings are considered the most 
important? Why? Do we decorate our buildings? 
How? Why? What do our buildings tell us about our 
local climate? 
Remind students that a study of the architecture of 
Ancient Greece is more than simply looking at pictures 
of buildings; it can actually reveal much about their 
culture and about the way they lived. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet ‘Building Ancient Greece’ introduces 
students to features of Ancient Greek architecture. 
They should then work in small groups to complete the 
questions on the Activity sheet ‘Building then and now’ 
which asks students to compare and contrast ancient 
and modern building methods. 
The Resource sheet ‘Ancient Greek houses’ 
provides information on the features of Ancient Greek 
neighbourhoods, houses and furniture. Students should 
read through this information, then work with a partner 
to complete the Activity sheet ‘Houses then and now’, 
which invites them to compare and contrast these 
features with those of modern houses. If time permits, 
responses could be shared with the class. 
The Resource sheet ‘The Parthenon (1)’ provides 
information on this famous building. Students then 
complete the Activity sheet ‘The Parthenon (2)’ to 
summarise what they have learnt.
Extension activity
Students could work in small groups to build a model 
of a famous Ancient Greek building. They could 
conduct their own research, develop drawings from 
different perspectives and build a model using recycled 
materials (such as used tissue boxes, toilet paper rolls, 
matchboxes, etc). 
Answers
Building Ancient Greece 1 practical, columns, simple, 
fancier, theatres, educated, sculptures, architecture, ornate.
The Parthenon (2) large, honouring, most, eight, relief

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
55
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Pericles
Objectives
l To explore the life and contributions of  
Pericles, one of the most significant leaders  
of Ancient Greece
l To introduce students to the concept  
of primary and secondary sources in  
historical study
l To encourage students to interpret a  
primary source
Prior knowledge
Students should have completed unit 1 (and 
preferably also unit 3) prior to commencing 
this section. They should have at least a basic 
understanding of the way the city-state of Athens 
was governed, and have heard of the Parthenon 
and the Acropolis.
Background
Ancient Greece became as strong and successful a 
civilisation as it did thanks largely to the efforts of 
numerous significant individuals. One of those was 
Pericles, a dominant political figure of Athens. Not 
only did Pericles lead the rebuilding of Athens after 
the second Persian War, but he also argued strongly 
in favour of democracy at a time when it was not the 
norm in Athens. 
Starter activity
Ask students to brainstorm as many significant figures 
as they can think of from the twentieth and twenty-
first centuries. What made these people significant? 
What did they do that we still remember them for; 
even when (in many cases) they’ve been dead for 
years? Discuss with students the fact that Ancient 
Greece became the notable civilisation that it was 
because of the many people who made a difference 
to Ancient Greek society. One of those people was 
Pericles. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet ‘Who was Pericles?’ provides 
students with information which they consolidate by 
completing the cloze activity on the Activity sheet 
‘What did Pericles do?’ 
The Resource sheet ‘Pericles’ Funeral Oration’ 
introduces students to the term primary source and 
presents them with a famous example. They should 
then work in pairs to complete the Activity sheet 
‘Interpreting a primary source’.
Extension activity
Pericles was a noted orator. He was very careful about 
his use of language and about choosing the most 
appropriate words to get his thoughts across and to 
convince people to support his ideas. His speeches 
were so famous that they’ve survived for thousands of 
years and are still very relevant. Ask students to choose 
a contemporary issue they feel passionate about and to 
write a speech that tries to convince the rest of the class 
of their point of view. Students then read their speeches 
out to the class. 
Answers
What did Pericles do? 2 Pericles, Athens, orator, 
democracy, Thucydides, Persian, Acropolis, Parthenon, 
Piraeus

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
60
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – The legacies of Ancient Greece
Objectives
l To learn about several significant legacies of 
Ancient Greece which influence the modern 
world: the Olympic Games, the concept of 
democracy, Aesop’s fables and mathematical 
discoveries
Prior knowledge
Students should be familiar with the names of  
Zeus and Hera, and know where the Olympic 
Games were held. 
Background
The Ancient Greek era was a time of prolific 
intellectual and cultural growth, the influences of 
which can still be felt today. In the study of history 
in general, it is important for students to recognise 
the significance and relevance of the past in creating 
the present; Ancient Greece provides many concrete 
examples of this relationship between past and 
present. 
Starter activity
Write the question ‘What is a legacy?’ on the board 
and ask students to respond. Encourage students 
to guess or make suggestions, even if they are not 
sure. If students do not come up with the right 
definition, give it to them: a legacy is anything that 
is left by predecessors or ancestors. Are legacies 
always a good thing? Can they sometimes be bad? 
Can students think of any legacies left to them by 
their parents and grandparents? Can they think 
of legacies left to the nation as a whole by past 
generations? Reinforce the idea that the past 
influencing the present is one of the reasons that 
history is such an important subject.
Resources and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet ‘The Olympic Games’ contains a 
cloze activity that gives students information about the 
origins of the Olympic Games. Once they have answered 
the final question (about the benefits of the Olympic 
Games) ask students to share one of their three benefits 
with the class. Write these contributions on the board.
The Activity sheet ‘Democracy’ begins with 
information on democracy in Ancient Greece and then 
gives students some reflection questions. They should 
work with a partner to complete these. They are also 
prompted to design a poster to be shared with the 
class. These can be displayed in the classroom or even 
throughout the school.
After reading the Resource sheet ‘Aesop’s fables’ 
students can work with a partner to complete the 
questions. Some students may not be familiar with the 
fables ‘The tortoise and the hare’ or ‘The boy who cried 
wolf’ (although this is unlikely) – you could recap the 
stories for them briefly, or pair students who haven’t 
heard of those fables with students who have. Students 
might like to share their fables with the rest of the class. 
The Activity sheet ‘It’s all in the numbers’, on 
mathematics, can be completed by students 
individually. 
Extension activity
Some people think that history is not relevant to the 
present. This activity is designed to encourage students 
to consider the continuing relevance of historical study 
(which includes looking at evidence and analysing the 
material found) by seeing both sides. Divide the class 
in half. One half of the class will argue that that ‘history 
is dead and irrelevant’ and the other half will argue 
that ‘our history affects our present and is relevant’. Set 
the debate up so that for each argument presented 
someone has a chance to make a counterargument. 
Answers
The Olympic Games Olympic, Women, wrestling, Zeus, 
Hera, Olympia, four, calendar, occurred, thousand, 
Roman, 1896, different, four, events

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
6
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Map of Ancient Greece
 
● Greece is located on a peninsula, a piece of land surrounded mainly by water. 
Greece has a very long coastline with inlets, bays and harbours. Ancient Greece, 
which was known at the time as Hellas, also included many islands found in the 
Aegean Sea, the Ionian Sea and the Mediterranean Sea. As a result, the Ancient 
Greeks used boats a lot – for travel, trade and fighting in wars. 
 
● The terrain of Greece is very mountainous, which made farming and travel over land 
difficult for the Ancient Greeks. The highest mountain in Greece is Mount Olympus, 
which was thought to be the home of the Gods. The Olympic Games weren’t held 
there – they were held in Olympia.
 
● Ancient Greece was much larger than the country we now know as Greece. It was 
made up of many separate poleis spread out over a vast area. A polis is a city-
state – each major city formed the centre of a separate state with its own laws 
and government. Most of the poleis were in the area we now know as Greece, 
but there were also some across the Aegean Sea, on the western coast of Persia. 
The boundaries of Ancient Greece changed many times over the centuries, as the 
Ancient Greeks conquered or lost land in wars.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
8
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Farming in a Mediterranean climate (1)
Greece has a Mediterranean climate. 
Resource sheet – Land and sea
Summer
Hot and very dry. 
Almost no  
rain at all. 
Spring
Weather warms  
up and rain 
continues. Lots  
of lush, green 
growth.
Autumn
Weather gets  
cooler. It begins  
to rain a little. 
Winter
Mild to cool.  
Most of the rain  
falls now. 
 
● Most people in Ancient Greece made their living from farming. We know this 
because the Ancient Greeks painted lots of pictures about the role of farming in 
their lives.  
 
● Farming in Ancient Greece wasn’t easy. The soil was very rocky and dry, and it was 
hard to grow crops. The mountains also made it difficult for farmers and traders 
to travel long distances. 
 
● Fresh water was scarce, especially in summer, so farmers had to grow crops that 
needed very little water. However, their warm climate and mild winters did have 
one advantage – they could grow different crops at different times of the year, 
not only in summer.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
9
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Farming in a Mediterranean climate (2)
 
● Farmers in Ancient Greece grew wheat and barley, olives, figs and grapes. 
The grapes could be eaten fresh, dried to make sultanas, or fermented in pottery 
jars to make wine. The olives could be eaten, or pressed to make olive oil. Olive oil 
was used for cooking and lighting. 
 
● Because Ancient Greece had lots of islands and a long coastline, there was easy 
access to the sea. As a result, the Ancient Greeks were great seafarers and many 
of them were fishermen. Fishermen caught fish, octopus, oysters and prawns.
 
● The rocky land made it hard to keep livestock such as cattle and pigs, so meat was 
very expensive and most people didn’t eat it. Farmers kept chickens, goats and 
sheep. They also kept some dairy cows. Milk was mainly used to make cheese. 
 
● Some farmers also 
kept bees for honey, 
in beehives made of 
terracotta. The Ancient 
Greeks did not have 
sugar, so honey was 
used as a sweetener. 
 
● A typical daily diet 
for someone living in 
Ancient Greece might 
have been: 
 •  breakfast – wheat 
or barley bread 
dipped in wine, and 
sometimes porridge
 • lunch – bread dipped in wine, with olives, cheese and some fruit
 •  dinner – the main meal of the day, it might include fish, vegetables, fruit, eggs,  
and honey cakes for dessert.

eat. We also use bread  
to scoop up food and to  
clean our hands.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
12
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Origins of Ancient Greece
The Bronze and Dark Ages
The Bronze Age (from around 3650 to 1600 BCE)
The Bronze Age refers to the period when people began to use copper and tin to make 
bronze objects such as weapons. In Ancient Greece, there were several significant stages 
within the Bronze Age. 
Two major civilisations of this time were the Minoans and the Mycenaeans.
The Minoans
The Minoans settled on the island of Crete in about 2500 BCE. They were named after their 
leader, King Minos. Copper and tin were plentiful on Crete, and the Minoans used these 
metals to make bronze weapons. The Minoans were a very advanced civilisation. They 
built excellent sewer and drainage systems, as well as roads to travel between cities. They 
were also famous for their ships.
The Mycenaeans
Around 1400 BCE, the Mycenaeans (from the north-east of the Peloponnese) conquered 
the Minoans. The Mycenaeans developed a thriving economy. They built forts in the 
hills with very thick and high walls. The forts were used as lookouts and to protect the 
Mycenaeans from invasion. Mycenaean military officers ruled their society and were 
highly respected. Like the Minoans, they made weapons from stone and bronze.
The Dark Ages of Ancient Greece (from around 1200 to 800 BCE)
 
● From approximately 1000 BCE, the Dorians, from the north, invaded Mycenae, as 
well as other parts of the Peloponnese, such as Corinth, Olympia and Sparta. The 
Dorians used weapons made of iron.  
 
● The Mycenaeans and Minoans had always recorded their history, but the Dorians 
were different. They had no written language and they did not paint pictures. When 
the Dorians invaded Greek cities, writing and painting stopped, because people 
were more worried about escaping than recording anything. It was many centuries 
before writing and painting became common again. This period of Greek history is 
known as the Dark Ages of Ancient Greece.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
14
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Landscape and the development  
of Athens
 
● The polis (city-state) of Athens was originally located on the Acropolis, which is a 
large, flat rock 150 metres above sea level. The Ancient Greeks considered it to be 
sacred. The top of the Acropolis has a surface area of 30 000 square metres. That’s 
almost as large as four soccer fields.
 
● Over time Athens grew beyond the Acropolis, but Athenians still built their most 
important buildings and temples on the Acropolis. One of the most important 
buildings in all of Ancient Greece – the Parthenon – was located there. There was 
also a temple to the goddess Athena and a theatron (theatre). The Ancient Greeks 
built a large wall to protect the Acropolis.
 
● Athens is located only 4 kilometres from the sea ports of Piraeus and Phaleron, which 
meant that the Athenians had easy access to the Aegean Sea, the Sea of Crete and 
the Mediterranean Sea. It was an easy, flat journey from Athens to either of these 
ports. The road to the ports was also protected by three walls. These protective 
walls and the flat land around Athens made it easy to watch out for invaders and to 
endure sieges. The mountain ranges a bit further out also helped protect Athens.
Resource sheet – Origins of Ancient Greece
978 1 92209 043 0

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
15
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Landscape and the development  
of Sparta
 
● The Ancient Greek polis (city-state) of Sparta was located in the Eurotas Valley, in 
the south-eastern Peloponnese. The valley is bordered on almost all sides by large 
mountains – Taygetos (2407 metres high) to the west, Parnon (1940 metres high) 
to the east. The northern border of Sparta is separated from Arcadia by another 
mountain range. These mountains acted like walls, making access to Sparta difficult. 
This is one of the reasons that Sparta was never attacked. The mountains also 
helped protect Sparta from winds and storms.
 
● The Eurotas river 
flows through 
the Eurotas Valley. 
It provided the 
Spartiates (people 
of Sparta) with 
fertile land for 
farming crops. It 
also provided them 
with drinking water 
and water for their 
animals. Food was 
plentiful in Sparta. 
 
● Sparta was not as 
close to a bay or 
sea as Athens. The 
Spartiates had to travel 46 kilometres to reach the sea port of Gythio. The journey 
to the port was not an easy walk (like it was for the Athenians). The port itself was 
also not as large and protected as either Piraeus Harbour or the port of Phaleron. 
As a result, the sea port of Gythio was used only for delivering supplies to Sparta.
Resource sheet – Origins of Ancient Greece

Activity sheet – Origins of Ancient Greece
Barriers to expansion
Mountains, fast-flowing rivers and great expanses of sea and ocean all made it 
difficult for the Ancient Greeks to get from one part of Greece to another. That’s why 
independent poleis (city-states) formed throughout Ancient Greece and why it was 
difficult for Greeks to feel united as a nation for so many centuries.
Athens and Sparta became two of the greatest poleis of Ancient Greece. Both the 
Athenians and the Spartiates tried to make the best of the natural features where  
they lived.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
18
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Politics and governance
Governing the poleis
Ancient Greece was made up of lots of city-states. Each city-state was called a polis –  
the plural is poleis. Each polis had its own laws and was independent of any other 
polis. The Ancient Greeks, who were called the Hellenes, spent most of their lives 
in their own polis. They only got together as a nation during times of war (such as 
the Persian Wars) and for big cultural games (such as the Olympic Games). The most 
powerful poleis of Ancient Greece were Corinth, Sparta and Athens.
Citizenship
The Ancient Greeks believed that citizenship was very important. However, not everyone 
could be a citizen. Not only did a citizen of a polis have to be born in that polis, but they 
also had to be a wealthy adult male. Slaves, women, peasants and migrants were not 
allowed to be citizens.
The Ancient Greeks believed it made sense that citizens of a polis had more rights than  
people who weren’t citizens. Only citizens were allowed to vote. Men had more rights  
than women, because the Ancient Greeks believed that men were smarter and stronger 
than women. The role of the leaders in each polis was to uphold these beliefs and the 
rights of citizens. 
The forms of government differed between poleis, but there were four main types 
of government:
 
●aristocracies, where the polis was ruled by wealthy, noble families
 
● dictatorships, where the polis was ruled by an individual (a dictator, who in 
Ancient Greece was known as a tyrant)
 
●oligarchies, where the polis was ruled by a small number of people
 
●democracies, where the polis was ruled by the citizens.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
20
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Politics and governance
Spartan oligarchy 
An oligarchy is a system of government in which only a few people rule. The most famous 
– and complicated – oligarchy was in Sparta. The flowchart below shows how many 
groups were involved in governing Sparta and what they each did.
Ephorate
The ephorate was made up of five ephors  
(governors or leaders) who were elected annually  
by the people. The ephorate ran Sparta.  
They could even put a king on trial.
Dual monarchy
Sparta had two kings. They performed religious duties,  
acted as judges and led the Spartan army. They also  
served on the council.
Council
The council of Sparta was made up of 30 noble elders 
(including the kings). The Council made important decisions 
and acted as a high court. It was run by the ephorate.
Assembly
The assembly was made up of all the male citizens  
(over 20 years old) of Sparta. They met once a month and 
voted on major issues. They usually followed the advice  
of the ephorate, who chaired the meetings.
978 1 92209 043 0

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
21
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Politics and governance
Athenian democracy 
The word democracy means ‘rule by the people’. Athenian democracy was one 
of the first known examples of democracy. In Athenian democracy, there was not a 
particular person who was the ruler. Instead, a public assembly of all male citizens 
(over 20 years of age) would meet 40 times a year. The assembly voted on issues to 
do with the running of the polis. The assembly in Athens was enormous – at least 
6000 men had to attend. 
The assembly
 
● The assembly also had nine archons (chief magistrates or judges). The archons 
were chosen by lottery and served for one year. Each archon looked after a certain 
group of issues and made sure things ran smoothly. 
 
● The decisions of the assembly were passed on to the council, which was known 
as the boule. The boule was made up of 500 men, each of them chosen from 
a lottery and required to serve for one year. Only Athenian male citizens who 
were over 30 years of age were able to serve on the council. The council wrote 
up the agenda for the assembly, and also carried out the decisions made by the 
assembly. They met almost every day in chambers in the agora (a meeting place 
in the centre of Athens) to discuss the running of Athens.
 
● Athens was an example of direct democracy. Direct democracy occurs  
when citizens are able to put across their own points of view and vote on each  
policy individually.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
25
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Everyday life
Social strata
Both Athens and Sparta had rules about who was important in their society. This created different social levels called 
strata. Athens and Sparta each had their own social strata.
Athens
Sparta
Citizens (men only). Types of citizens included:
 
● thetes (mainly craftsmen who did not own land)
 
● hoplites (mainly farmers who owned armour)
 
●knights (rich men with war horses)
 
● pentakosiomedemnoi (very rich men who gave 
money to the army).
Two Kings, one from each of the two royal lines.
Metics – non-citizen families who migrated to Athens.  
They often traded between Athens and their homeland.  
Men tended to trade with other men, and so it was the  
male metics who ran the family businesses.
Spartiates – male citizens who had been born 
in Sparta, were over 30 years old and had been 
through the agoge (Sparta’s education and 
training system for boys). The wives and daughters 
of Spartiates were also called Spartiates, but they 
were not considered citizens or allowed to vote.
Freedmen – men who had once been slaves but had  
been freed as a reward for their loyalty. Only male  
slaves could be granted their freedom as all women  
(whether slaves or citizens) were always under the  
control of a man. The only way a female slave  
could be freed was if she was allowed to marry  
a non-slave male.
Perioeci – craftsmen and women, who 
could not vote, even though they paid 
tax. Perioeci men sometimes served in 
the military, but as they had not been 
through the agoge they were not 
considered citizens. 
Slaves – Male slaves were often used as  
rowers on triremes (three-decked boats).  
Female slaves helped with household chores.
Helots – male and female slaves 
who worked the land and helped 
with household chores.

Family life in Athens
Life in Ancient Greece was very different, depending on whether you were male or  
female, and which city you lived in. Men and women led very different lives, and male  
and female children had very different childhoods. This also varied between cities.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1

© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Warfare
The hoplites and the phalanx 
Ancient Greek soldiers were known as hoplites. The best hoplites came from Sparta. 
 
● Hoplites had only two weapons: a long spear (doru) and a short sword (xiphos).  
They also used a large round shield (hoplon) made of wood and covered in leather 
and bronze. They wore metal guards called greaves on their skins and a metal 
breastplate called a cuirass. On their heads they wore a metal helmet.
 
● Hoplites had to buy their own armour. Rich men had armour made of metal. Poor 
men often made their armour by gluing together layers of cloth. Sometimes they 
wore no armour at all and simply went into battle carrying their shield and a spear. 
A phalanx
Hoplites fought in a military formation known as a phalanx. A phalanx was formed 
by lining up hoplites into rows known as ranks. Each rank had roughly 12 men.  
There were usually eight to ten ranks in a phalanx, all lined up behind one another.
Hoplites in the first few ranks pointed their spears out in front. The rest of the 
hoplites pointed their spears overhead. All of the hoplites locked their shields  
together to create a solid barrier that would protect them from enemy arrows.  
The phalanx moved slowly – no faster than walking pace – so it could stay in 
formation.

formidable sight. We look like a massive, 
slow moving creature. Our dorus look like 
long spikes sticking out everywhere,  
and our hoplons seem like  
enormous scales.

The Battle of Marathon 
The Ancient Greeks didn’t shy away from battle, even when they were outnumbered. 
At the Battle of Marathon, 10 000 Greek hoplites faced 20 000 Persian soldiers – and won! 
The Persians, led by King Darius, had threatened to invade Athens. The Athenians were 
so worried that they began evacuating the city. 
Before the battle began, Pheidippides – an Athenian hoplite – ran from Athens to 
Sparta to get help. It took him two days and two nights to get there and he ran all the 
way – 240 kilometres. He didn’t stop to rest after that. Instead, he fought long and hard 
at Marathon. Then, when the Greeks had defeated the Persians, he ran all the way from 
Marathon to Athens (42 kilometres) to tell everyone the good news.  Poor Pheidippides 
died from exhaustion when he got to Athens, but his legend lives on.

Resource sheet – Religion
Ancient Greek mythology
The gods were a very important part of Ancient Greek life. The people of Ancient Greece 
believed that many gods ruled Greece and that they would be punished by the gods if they 
did anything wrong. 
The word myth simply means ‘story’. Ancient Greek myths were basically a rich collection 
of stories involving Gods, heroes and humans. All three were important and all three 
interacted with each other, but they were each very different.
 
● Gods were immortal. There were two types of gods: the Titans and the Olympians. 
The Titans were giants, and the mountains of Greece were their thrones. The Olympians 
lived on Mount Olympus, but they loved to meddle in the lives of humans. Sometimes 
they even fell in love with humans and had children with them. Gods could not control 
humans, because humans have free will, but they could make life hard or easy for them. 
 
● Heroes were mortal. They had one parent who was a god and one who was human. 
Even though great myths existed about heroes such as Achilles, they still lived among 
the people in Ancient Greece. 
 
● Humans were also (obviously) mortal. Even though they were not heroes or 
gods, they were still able to fall in love with them. The gods thought humans were 
interesting and attractive. 
The first generation of Ancient Greek gods were the Titans. 
They were known as the Elders. There were 12 original Titans. 
The first were Uranus (the sky) and Gaia (the Earth). Together 
they had many children, most of whom ruled with them. 
Eventually the Titans were challenged by the Olympians 
for the power to rule over Greece. The Olympians were the 
children of the Titans.
A war then took place between the Titans and the Olympians. 
This war was known as the Battle of the Titans. 
The Olympians won the battle and they became the new gods.

Athena and Arachne
Athena was the goddess of wisdom, war and crafts. She was very clever and could 
make amazing things. One day Athena heard about a young woman called Arachne. 
Arachne was a very talented weaver and was proud of her skill. She had even dared 
to think that her weaving was better than Athena’s. Athena heard this and was 
annoyed. She dressed up as an old woman and paid Arachne a visit.
When asked by the old woman if she thought her skill was better than the goddess 
Athena, Arachne said ‘yes’. The old woman then revealed that she was really Athena, 
but Arachne refused to be intimidated. 
Athena challenged Arachne to a weaving contest and Arachne accepted. Athena 
wove a beautiful tapestry that showed the gods doing good things. Arachne’s 
tapestry showed the gods being selfish and unkind.
Athena was so angry with Arachne for disrespecting the gods that she hit Arachne. 
Then she felt sorry for her. Instead of killing her, Athena turned Arachne into the first 
spider, so that she could spend her life weaving. 
That’s how it came to be that spiders belong to the class of animals called ‘arachnids’.

Theatre 
Drama was an important part of daily life for the people of Ancient Greece. The plays 
were mainly about the gods, and they would be performed in front of large crowds in an 
outdoor theatre called a theatron. 
Each polis (city-state) had a theatron. Theatrons were enormous and able to fit 
thousands of people at a time. They were usually built on hillsides, so that people sitting in 
the back rows could see the stage. 
Plays were considered so important that poleis (city-states) competed with each other 
to see who had the best playwrights and performers. One of the most famous playwrights 
was Sophocles. He wrote more than 100 plays.
The actors were always men. They wore colourful 
costumes and dramatic masks to help the audience identify 
different characters. The actors didn’t speak. Instead, the story 
was sung by a choir. 
+ 1    Label the different parts of a Greek theatron.
+  2    Draw your own dramatic mask. Keep in mind that the mask needs to show a lot 
of things. For example, is your character happy, sad or angry? Is it young or old? 
Is it male or female? How will you design your mask so that the audience knows 
these things just by looking at the mask?
 
3    Think of three ways in which Ancient Greek theatre is different to theatre today 
and write your answers in your workbook.

Sculpture
The Ancient Greeks loved to build large statues, especially of their gods. They also 
produced lots of two-dimensional sculptures on the sides of buildings – these are called 
relief sculptures. 
The most famous of the Ancient Greek relief sculptures were made by Phidias for the 
Parthenon, a huge temple in Athens. Phidias, with the help of other sculptors, made relief 
sculptures that went all the way around the Parthenon. 
The Ancient Greeks worshipped perfection. Their statues of humans and gods  
focused on the perfect human body. Muscles were defined and male bodies were often 
shown nude. 
Most Ancient Greek statues were carved out of marble and limestone. Not many of 
them still exist, although we know what they looked like because the Ancient Romans 
made copies of them and those copies still survive today.

47

Achieve!
Activity sheet – Art
Music
The Ancient Greeks believed that music was a blessing. They thought the gods had 
invented many of their instruments and they believed that playing music brought them 
closer to the gods. Music could be heard at almost every ceremony and public event, 
including sporting events. People sang a lot, and choirs provided much of the music 
during Ancient Greek plays. 
Instruments
The lyre was a stringed instrument with a round, 
hollow part that was usually made using a tortoise 
shell. It was played by strumming or plucking the 
strings with a plectrum (or pick). There was also 
a larger version of the lyre, called a kithara. The 
kithara was much bigger and made of wood. 
The aulos was made of two reeds. It was 
played by blowing into the reeds. It was very 
hard to play the aulos because the reeds 
were very narrow. 
The syrinx was made by tying together pipes of 
different lengths. It was played by blowing across 
the top of the pipes. 
+ 1    Name some instruments that we have 
today that look like the lyre, aulos or syrinx. 
+ 2    When do we use music in our modern 
culture? How does this compare to the way 
the Ancient Greeks used music?

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
51
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Architecture
Ancient Greek houses
Early Greek houses were usually made of wood, clay bricks or stone, and were very basic. 
They had two or three rooms and sometimes a courtyard. Roofs were made of reeds or 
clay tiles. The floors of most houses were tiled using clay tiles or pebbles. 
Over time, the style of houses changed. Rich people had very large houses with many 
rooms. The houses of poor people remained small and basic. 
Courtyards were very important. They allowed people to be outdoors and still within 
the privacy of their homes. Women spent most of their time at home, so the courtyard 
gave them an opportunity to be outside without leaving their house. Protection was also 
very important to the Ancient Greeks, so most houses were surrounded by high stone 
walls and strong gates. 
Neighbourhoods were usually made up of five or six houses lined up next to each 
other along a straight road. These houses usually shared a common wall, much like 
modern townhouses. There would often be one house that stood alone in the middle of 
a neighbourhood and was bigger and more ornate than the others. This house belonged 
to wealthy people. 
Ancient Greek furniture was very practical. There were lots of stools, chairs and tables 
for cooking and eating. Beds were made of rope stretched across a wooden frame. 
Mattresses were stuffed with dry leaves and grasses. Fireplaces kept families warm in 
winter, and were used for cooking and to heat water for bathing.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
53
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Architecture
The Parthenon (1)
The temples of Ancient Greece were very impressive. The gods were very important to 
the Ancient Greeks and they wanted to honour them through the temples they built. 
Temples were some of the largest buildings in a polis. They were rectangular structures 
with columns across the front. Most temples had six columns and were decorated with 
a frieze – a band of relief sculptures around the perimeter of a building. A temple would 
also have a pediment, the decorated triangular part at the front of the temple. 
The most impressive Ancient Greek temple ever built was the Parthenon. The 
Parthenon was built on top of the Acropolis, the highest hill in Athens. It was built around 
440 BCE to honour the goddess Athena. 
The architects who designed the Parthenon wanted it to be the best temple ever.  
They wanted it to be enormous and they wanted it built entirely out of marble. They 
gave it eight columns across the front instead of the usual six. They also gave it a very 
decorative frieze. The frieze of the Parthenon depicted the gods and told mythological 
stories using pictures.
