ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
56
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Pericles
Who was Pericles?
Pericles lived between 495 and 429 BCE. He 
was one of the most important leaders of 
Ancient Greece. He was born in Athens and 
entered political life as a young man. 
Pericles was a well-educated man and 
he understood the power of words. He was 
very careful about what he said and the 
way he said it. His speeches, which aimed 
to inspire Athenians, were even recorded 
by Thucydides, a famous Ancient Greek 
historian who lived at the time of Pericles. 
Pericles believed that Athens was the 
greatest polis (city-state) of Ancient Greece. 
His speeches (also called orations) were 
designed to make people feel good about 
Athens and its people. Pericles spoke of how important Athens was to the evolution 
of Ancient Greece. He also spoke of the importance of democracy and did his best to 
convince people it was a good thing.
Pericles believed in the value of things like buildings, roads and temples. He felt that 
these things showed the values and wealth of a society. He also felt that buildings should 
be useful as well as attractive. For example, he convinced the Athenians that it would be a 
good idea to build walls to protect the road from Athens to the port of Piraeus. 
During the second Persian War, Athens was attacked by the Persian army. The Athenians 
had fled Athens during this attack, leaving many of its buildings to be destroyed by 
the Persian army. Eventually the Greeks defeated the Persians and resettled in Athens, 
but many of their buildings and temples had been destroyed. Pericles was in charge of 
rebuilding many of these, including the Parthenon on the Acropolis.

Resource sheet – Pericles
Pericles’ Funeral Oration
Historians use primary and secondary sources to better understand historical events. 
A primary source is something that was produced during the historical period being 
studied. Some examples of primary sources include buildings and artefacts (things made 
by people), such as statues, pottery, and things that people said and which were recorded  
at the time. 
A secondary source is something that was produced after the historical period being 
studied has ended. 
Speeches (or orations) made by Pericles and recorded at the time by an Ancient Greek 
historian, Thucydides, are examples of primary sources. Below is an excerpt from the 
Funeral Oration given by Pericles at the end of the first year of the Peloponnesian war. 
This oration was in honour of the Athenians that had been killed during the war. 
I will speak first of our  
ancestors, for it is right and seemly that  
now, when we are lamenting (mourning)  
the dead, a tribute (a sign of respect) should be  
paid to their memory. There has never been a time 
when they did not inhabit (live in) this land, which by 
their valour (bravery) they will have handed down from 
generation (a group of people born around the same 
time) to generation, and we have received from them  
a free state. But if they were worthy of praise, still more 
were our fathers, who added to their inheritance 
(something that is handed down after death), and  
after many a struggle transmitted (passed  
on) to us their sons this great empire  
(a powerful country or region).

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Greece 1
62
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Activity sheet – The legacies of Ancient Greece 
Democracy
The Athenians of Ancient Greece created democracy, a system of government that gives 
everyone equal say. Aristotle, an Ancient Greek philosopher who lived in Athens, was a 
great believer in democracy. He said it was ‘rule by the people’. However, not all people 
in Ancient Greece were allowed to be a part of the political process. Only free men could 
vote. Women, children, migrants and slaves could not. 
The Athenians used a form of democracy known as direct democracy. This meant that 
voters were involved in every part of ruling a country. They discussed and voted on each 
issue separately, and anybody could raise an issue.
Democracy is still considered very important. In fact, most people believe that 
democracy is the only fair way to rule. 
The most common form of democracy today is representative democracy. 
Representative democracy is where the people vote for their representatives. Those 
representatives form government and make decisions.
Democracy tries to include all people. It is based on fairness and equality. It demands 
that people be heard and treated well. Democracy also requires that people participate 
by voting and by being informed.
+ 1   Do you think democracy is important? Explain why or why not?

information (either in words or pictures) about the following:
 
●democracy from Ancient Greece
 
●what democracy provides (for example, a fair system of government)
 
●what democracy demands (for example, participation such as voting).

Achieve!
Resource sheet – The legacies of Ancient Greece 
Aesop’s fables
Aesop was an Ancient Greek slave. He wrote fables, which are stories with a message or 
moral. More than 2000 years after he died, we still read these fables. Here is one of them.
The dog and the wolf
One day, a wolf met a dog. The wolf was starving and hadn’t eaten for weeks. His 
body was thin and his ribs poked out. The dog, on the other hand, was rather plump. 
The dog took pity on the wolf. ‘My poor friend,’ he said, ‘Come home with me and 
my master will feed you well. He feeds me every day and look how healthy I am.’
The wolf was very grateful. ‘Thank you, dog,’ he said. 
The two began walking towards the dog’s home. After a while, the wolf noticed 
a bare patch on the dog’s neck. ‘My friend,’ asked the wolf, ‘what happened to your 
neck? I notice that your fur is worn away there. Were you in a fight?’
‘Oh no,’ laughed the dog. ‘My master chains up his dogs at night and the chain 
rubs the back of my neck.’ Seeing the worried look on the wolf’s face, the dog 
quickly added, ‘Don’t worry. It doesn’t hurt and you’ll get used to the chain quickly 
enough.’
The wolf stopped still, thanked the dog for his 
kindness, then turned and walked away. ‘Where 
are you going?’ called the dog.
‘I would rather die a free wolf than live as a  
well-fed slave,’ said the wolf.
+ 1    What do you think is the moral of this fable? (What are we supposed to learn 
from it?)
__________________________________________________________________________
__________________________________________________________________________
__________________________________________________________________________
+ 2     Write your own version of one of Aesop’s fables. You can find more in the library 
or on the internet. You could also try making up a fable of your own – use 
animals, like Aesop did, and make sure it has a moral.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Rome 1
5
© Chrissie Michaels and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Objectives
l To sequence how Rome was formed and 
describe how physical features such as the 
Seven Hills and the River Tiber influenced the 
early settlement of Rome
l To identify and describe examples of written 
and material evidence used by modern 
historians to build a picture of Rome’s 
formation
l To use an example from traditional  
storytelling about the foundation of Rome and 
to draw a conclusion about an early Roman 
religious belief 
Prior knowledge
Students should be able to find Italy on a map.  
They should understand the terms archaeologist 
and historian.
Background
Both the writing of historians from the ancient world 
and material evidence (structures and artefacts) 
shape our understanding of the formation of Rome. 
These also give us insight into the beliefs and 
practices of Ancient Romans.
The natural features of the area around Rome 
shaped its development. The Palatine Hill’s proximity 
to the lowest crossing point of the River Tiber was 
what most likely led to it eventually being selected 
as the site of the main city of Rome. 
Starter activity 
Begin by discussing with students what a legend is. 
Ask students to share some family stories and discuss 
how these may have changed over time. Brainstorm 
reasons why this may happen. Discuss what turns a 
story into a legend. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheets ‘Origins of Rome (1)’ and ‘Origins of 
Rome (2)’ provide information about where and how 
Rome started, based on natural features and material 
evidence. Students should complete these sheets 
and then complete the Activity sheet ‘Using material 
evidence’.
Read the Activity sheet ‘The legend of Romulus and 
Remus’ with the class, and then ask them to discuss how 
the legend makes Rome sound powerful and important. 
What evidence has been found that links to a legend 
about how Rome was founded? How much fact is found 
in legends?
Extension activity
Students could research the origins of their own city or 
town, and then write their own legend or myth about 
how it began.
Answers 
Using material evidence Artefacts: flint axes, funeral 
urns; Remains: Neanderthal skulls; Structures: Etruscan 
tomb; Natural features/landscape: Seven Hills, 
marshlands, River Tiber; Order: Groups live apart … 
Tribes drain … Rome becomes a city…
The legend of Romulus and Remus 1 Palatine Hill;  
2 Aventine Hill; 3 Rome became a city in 753 BCE; the 
Sabines were the first people to live in Rome; 4 Legends 
are fiction, but some may also include some facts.

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Rome 1
10
© Chrissie Michaels and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Roman society 
Objectives
l To identify, describe and compare two key 
groups in Ancient Roman society: the patricians 
and the plebeians
l To learn about dependency relationships and 
the laws of intermarriage
l To gain an overview of the Senate during the 
Republic, including who had the power to vote 
in elections and change laws
l To learn how a citizen might progress in a 
career through the Senate
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that societies generally 
involve a social hierarchy of some sort, and that 
one’s place in the hierarchy is determined by a 
range of factors, including birthplace, education, 
economic status and gender. 
Background
The Roman Republic was the second in the 
sequence of Rome’s governing bodies from kings 
to empire. It underpinned modern ideas of a 
democratic state by deliberately investing power in 
two leaders (consuls), giving the Senate a central role 
as powerbroker and administrator, and allowing its 
male citizens (patricians and plebeians) the right to 
vote for consuls, officials and laws. 
During the Republic, Roman citizens could 
improve their social status. For a plebeian 
(average Roman citizen), having a patron from the 
patrician (noble) class offered an opportunity for 
advancement. Plebeians were allowed to marry 
patricians. However, plebeians lost their right to 
become senators by the end of the Republic.
The pater familias (eldest male in the family) 
was the lawful head of the household in both social 
groups. Women could not become Roman citizens.
Starter activity
Ask students to think about how someone today can 
change their own life for the better, for instance through 
education, work or exercising the right to vote. Does 
everyone in our society have the same opportunities in 
life? What makes it difficult for some people to improve 
their lives? What do students understand by the term 
‘social class’?
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet ‘The Senate’ develops student 
knowledge about the two key groups of citizens 
(patricians and plebeians) during the Republic, and their 
right to vote for leaders and change laws. 
In the Activity sheet ‘A career in the Senate’, students 
consider how a male citizen might have advanced in a 
career through the Senate. 
The Resource sheets ‘Patricians’ and ‘Plebeians’ 
each present the two citizenship classes in Ancient 
Rome through the eyes of a family member. In the 
Activity sheet ‘Relationships in Roman society’, students 
identify and describe the status of the pater familias, 
patronage and the law of intermarriage. They conclude 
their study of patricians and plebeians, by comparing 
their everyday life in the Activity sheet ‘Plebeians and 
patricians’.
Extension activities
1 Hold a Roman-style mock election (placing a stone 
in a basket after crossing a bridge). Assign roles for 
students – patricians, plebeians, slaves, women, people 
from other places – and have them decide who may 
vote for two ‘consuls’ to represent the class.
2  With a partner, have students discuss how the 
following laws may have helped Ancient Romans to 
improve their social, political and economic standing  
in society. 
l  Some non-citizens of Rome can become citizens. 
l  A slave can become free.
l   A plebeian can sometimes hold office or obtain titles 
in the army, trade, and in religion.
Answers
A career in the Senate 1 No;  2 No;  3 No;  4 Yes;  5 Yes;  
6 (from bottom): protects; organises; judges; orders; 
rules; retires
Relationships in Roman society 1 patricians;  2 plebeians; 
3 patron;  4 slave;  5 patricians, plebeians, slaves;  6 females, 
slaves;  7 father, grandfather

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Rome 1
17
© Chrissie Michaels and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Julius Caesar
Objectives
l To identify and describe Julius Caesar, a 
significant figure in the history of Ancient Rome
l To draw conclusions about how public opinion at 
the time was divided over his success as a ruler
l To identify and describe what happened as a 
result of his assassination
Prior knowledge
Students should have completed Unit 2 and be 
familiar with the Roman Republic and the social 
structure of Rome.
Background
Julius Caesar was a powerful general who won many 
important battles and formed alliances through 
a string of marriages and liaisons. Some of his 
greatest achievements as ruler of Rome were the 
introduction of the Julian Calendar and a law reform 
against extortion. However, he also made many 
enemies, particularly when he changed the way 
Rome was ruled. He was appointed dictator of Rome 
and by no longer allowing elections, he was able 
to appoint his favourites to senior offices. Romans 
were divided in their loyalties: some supported him, 
others thought he was a tyrant. After his murder by 
a group of Senators on 15 March (the Ides of March) 
44 BCE, there were riots in the streets. Not long 
afterwards, Romans found themselves in the midst 
of a civil war. 
Starter activity
Begin by having students find Italy, France (Gaul), 
Britain and Egypt on a map of the northern 
hemisphere. Identify the Rubicon, which formed 
the boundary between Gaul and Italy. Inform the 
students that these were significant places in the life 
of Julius Caesar. Make sure students know that Gaul 
is the old name for France.
Resource and Activity sheets 
The Activity sheet ‘A powerful general and leader’ 
introduces students to the life of Julius Caesar. They 
then explore why the Senators committed their act 
of murder in the Activity sheet ‘Caesar’s murder’.  Two 
historical sources are presented to students for student 
reflection.
The Activity sheet ‘Caesar and Brutus’ asks students 
to reflect on Caesar’s career and Brutus’ reasons for 
acting against him. 
The Resource sheet ‘Vox Pop (1)’ presents Ancient 
Roman characters who reflect the divisions in popular 
opinion about the murder of Julius Caesar. In the 
Activity sheet ‘Vox pop (2)’, students then reflect on the 
range of opinions at the time and the consequences 
(civil war) of the political unrest set in motion by Julius 
Caesar’s murder.
Extension activities
Have students choose one of the following sayings 
and research its meaning: ‘Beware the Ides of March!’, 
‘Veni Vidi Vici’. Can they guess what they mean? In what 
situations might these phrases be used? Students can 
use the internet or the library to research these further. 
Imagine Brutus is being interviewed about his role in 
the murder of Julius Caesar. Have students work in pairs, 
with one as the interviewer asking the questions, and the 
other answering as Brutus. The interview should cover 
what happened, why Brutus took part, where the murder 
took place, how he felt when Caesar spoke to him in 
those final moments. Does Brutus have any regrets about 
what he and the other senators have done? 
Answers
A powerful general and leader 2, 9, 4, 7, 6, 3, 5, 1, 8
Caesar’s murder 1 The assassins have restored freedom 
to Rome. Julius Caesar is an enemy of Rome. March 15  
is an important day in Rome’s history. 2 Ides of March; 
Eid-Mar; 3 Suetonius. Roman coin.
Caesar and Brutus 1 Caesar became respected as a 
successful general by the people of Rome. 2 Caesar 
formed an alliance with two influential senators. 
3 Marriage and important friends helped Caesar 
strengthen his connections. 4 Caesar defeated Pompey 
with a loyal army backing him. 5 Caesar increased his 
number of supporters in the Senate. 6 Because they 
thought he wanted to rule alone.
Vox pop (2) 2 dismiss[ed] his bodyguards; 3 riot;  
4 civil war

23
© Chrissie Michaels and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – The Roman Legion 
Objectives
l To learn about the life of a Roman legionary 
and understand the strengths of the Roman 
army and how these led to their success  
in warfare
l To sequence some of the major battles and 
conquests from the Republic through to the 
fall of the western Roman Empire, and to locate 
empire strongholds on a map
l To understand how the Roman army helped  
to shape the known ancient world
Prior knowledge
Students should know that timelines can help 
them to sequence information and describe 
change or continuity over time.
Background
The Roman army is appreciated, not only as an 
integral part of the expansion, colonisation and 
building of the known ancient world, but for the 
legacy it left to the modern world. In the earlier days 
of the Roman Republic, soldiers were recruited for 
one battle at a time. After 107 BCE the army became 
a regular, long-term force. This professional army 
was led by senators of Rome as part of their duty to 
serve the people. The army continued to expand the 
Republic; then set about protecting Rome’s provinces. 
Among their many other contributions to the ancient 
world, they built a vast network of roads. The army’s 
main fighting unit was the highly organised, well-
trained and disciplined legion. 
Starter activity
Ask students why a country might have its own 
army. Record their answers (for example, to protect 
people and borders, to conquer) for referral 
throughout the unit. Ask them why they think the 
Roman army is still remembered? They can check 
their predictions as they work on the unit.
Resource and Activity sheets
The resources and activities in this unit provide a 
basic introduction to the life of a Roman legionary 
(foot soldier). The Resource sheets  ‘A Roman legion’ 
and ‘Uniform, weapons and training’ cover some of 
the factors that contributed to the success of the 
Roman army, most notably its organisation and the 
superiority of Roman weaponry and disciplined training 
techniques. Students reflect on these in the Activity 
sheet ‘An organised fighting unit’. 
Students then identify and describe the 
requirements and lifestyle of a legionary in the Activity 
sheet ‘Join a Roman legion!’, finishing with a timeline in 
the Activity sheet ‘Major wars and conquests’. 
Extension activities
Have students imagine that they are a young legionary 
stationed at an outpost far from Rome. Have them write 
a letter home to their family, letting them know which 
legion they are in and describing their daily life. What is 
different to life in Rome? What would they like sent to 
them from home? 
Consider in what ways the Roman army was well 
organised. As a class, discuss how the Roman army 
was able to invade so many countries and remain 
undefeated for a long time. Use these words as prompts: 
better weapons, well-organised, self-sufficient, good 
equipment, fit and healthy.
Answers
An organised fighting unit sandal; red tunic; spade; 
food and cooking pot; iron nails; gladius; wicker basket; 
pilium; shields; armour
Major wars and conquests 1 Spain, Gaul; 2 Britain;  
3 Dacia

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Rome 1
29
© Chrissie Michaels and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Slave or free
Objectives
l To gain an understanding of some examples of 
diversity and differences between key groups 
(Roman citizens, freedmen, women, slaves) 
l To identify and describe some examples of their 
rights and freedoms 
l To draw some conclusions about the prevailing 
Roman values and experience in relation to 
slavery and freedom
Prior knowledge
Students should know that in ancient times not all 
people had equal rights and that this remains the 
case in many societies today.
Background
In order to understand the nature of a society, it is 
important to look at its values. The Romans had a 
hierarchy of citizenship down to slavery. On all rungs, 
the status of a female was inferior to a male. Ancient 
Rome could not have grown so rapidly without its 
vast industry of slaves, who were used for building, 
food production and in all facets of daily life. 
Romans did believe that a slave could be set 
free. They recognised these freed slaves as a class 
(freedman and freedwoman) and in law. 
Starter activity
Ask students to brainstorm their responses to these 
questions: What are human rights? What does it 
mean to be free? Does slavery still happen today? 
Ask them to discuss the fact that 50 per cent of all 
females in the world today are illiterate.
Resource and Activity sheets
In the Resource sheet ‘Free-born citizens’ students 
identify and consider the differing rights of diverse 
groups in Ancient Rome, before reading about the 
experiences of being ‘Slaves’. Through the Activity sheet 
‘Slave or free?’ and ‘A slave’s work’ they focus on the 
various work duties required of a slave, and interpret 
what it meant to be a free-born citizen, slave, or 
freedman/woman in Roman times.
The Romans did believe a slave could be set free.  
The final activity ‘Free at last’ asks students to reflect on 
the likelihood of this happening. 
Extension activities
Slavery still exists today in some parts of the modern 
world. Students could research an example of 
contemporary slavery, such as child soldiers, cocoa 
harvesters in Africa or garment industry workers in 
India. As a class, discuss why slavery still exists. What 
actions could be taken to stop it? You could extend this 
discussion to include women’s illiteracy.
As a class, consider the following questions and hold 
a discussion.
l   Why do you think voting is considered such an 
important right to have?
l   How do you think Ancient Romans justified men 
having more rights than women?
Answers
A slave’s work 4, 3, 1, 2, 5

ACHIEVE!   History – The Ancient World: Rome 1
35
© Chrissie Michaels and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Gladiators
Objectives
l To identify and describe what it was like to be a 
gladiator
l To develop knowledge about the beliefs and 
values of Ancient Romans by considering 
the popularity and extent of their gladiator 
contests 
l To sequence how Roman attitudes and laws 
about gladiator combat changed over time 
l To describe some of the consequences of 
Roman gladiator combat on the wildlife in the 
known ancient world 
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of what is 
considered popular entertainment today.
Background
For all its sophistication and intelligence, Roman 
life had a side that was very brutal to our modern 
sensitivities. People valued the art of killing 
and gloried in savage blood sports such as the 
gladiatorial games. These contests date back to 
264 BCE as funeral matches to honour dead family 
members. Designed and often sponsored by the 
state as entertainment for the populace, gladiator 
contests attracted hundreds of thousands of 
spectators. One theory about their popularity is that 
because most Ancient Romans could not expect to 
live beyond 30, they felt it was important to meet 
death with glory and dignity. In a society based on 
the strength and courage of its army as a military 
force, the government may have wished to teach its 
citizens how to use combat and face death. As hard 
as it is for us to imagine, watching gladiators die 
‘well’ was a way to achieve this goal. Gladiators did 
rebel at times, one famous example being Spartacus. 
Towards the end of the empire, changing attitudes 
led to the eventual ban of gladiator sports by the 
emperor Honorius.
Starter activity
Ask students what they associate with the word 
‘gladiator’. Discuss how the word is used today. Discuss 
why we find it hard today to understand how gladiator 
games could be accepted. Discuss modern examples 
of controversial sports such as Spanish bullfighting or 
foxhunts. How do students feel about these?
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet ‘Gladiator combat’ and the Activity 
Sheet ‘Gladiator FAQ’ provide an overview of the topic. 
The Activity sheet ‘Wild animals in the arena’ gives 
students an opportunity to describe Roman attitudes 
about wild animals and consider the long-term effects 
on the animal world. 
The Activity sheet ‘Secutor’s fan club’ asks them to 
summarise, in interview form, the life of a gladiator.
The Activity sheet ‘Changing attitudes’ asks students 
to revise how attitudes to gladiatorial combat changed 
over time, and to think about how these values and 
beliefs compare with those of today. They should refer 
to the Resource sheet ‘Gladiator combat’ to complete 
the flowchart.
Extension activity
Ask students how we can make sense of the Ancient 
Romans’ enjoyment of human blood sports? Have 
them recall what they discussed in the starter activity. 
Have their views changed? What do other sports such 
as wrestling and boxing have in common with the 
gladiator games? Finish by deciding on a set of values 
that today’s society holds with regards to modern 
sports.
Answers
Wild animals in the arena Asia Minor (Turkey): tiger, 
leopard; Numidia (North Africa): rhinoceros, elephant; 
Aegyptus (Egypt):hippopotamus; Hibernia (Ireland): 
wolf; Caledonia (Scotland): bear; Mesopotamia (Iraq): 
lion

41
© Chrissie Michaels and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Pompeii 
Objectives
l To sequence the stages of the eruption of 
Vesuvius in 79 CE and describe the impact on 
Pompeii 
l To identify and describe examples of scientific 
and written evidence used to provide historical 
information about Pompeii and its inhabitants 
l To describe some aspects of Pompeiian  
daily life 
l To draw conclusions about how Pompeii is  
a unique example of ‘preserved history’
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic understanding of 
what archaeology is. They should also understand 
the concept of cause and effect.
Background
The catastrophic volcanic explosion at Pompeii in 
79 CE resulted in the town being preserved through 
the ages. Historical inquiry began with the first 
archaeological discovery at the site and subsequent 
record keeping, moving on to the present era of 
intense preservation and conservation. Today, 60 
per cent of the town is uncovered. World citizens are 
fortunate to be able to stroll through this unique 
open-air museum and observe evidence of what life 
was like for Pompeiians at the time Mount Vesuvius 
erupted. However, the need for constant upkeep 
of Pompeii was made apparent in late 2010, when 
several walls of the town collapsed.
Starter activity
Ask students what they know about volcanic 
eruptions. Locate Mount Vesuvius and Pompeii on  
a map of Italy.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet ‘Pompeii is buried’ gives an 
overview of the disaster, and then explains how the 
town came to be rediscovered and preserved. Once 
students have read this information, get them to 
complete the Activity sheet ‘Mount Vesuvius erupts’, 
where they sequence the key stages of the volcanic 
eruption and its effect on Pompeii. 
In the Activity sheet ‘A personal view of Pompeii’ 
students read a recount from Pliny the Younger. They 
are then asked to complete an empathy task, in which 
they imagine being an eyewitness to the destruction 
of Pompeii. You could extend this activity further by 
holding a class discussion about modern disasters and 
the emotional effects on survivors and rescuers. 
The Resource sheet ‘Pompeii casts’ explains how 
Fiorelli’s method of using plaster casts has contributed 
to the ongoing scientific preservation and conservation 
of Pompeii. In the Activity sheet ‘Daily life in Pompeii’, 
students imagine and interpret the daily lives of these 
Ancient Pompeiians based on what has been found and 
preserved.
Finally, in ‘Cause and effect’ students sum up the 
knowledge they have gained in the unit, before reflecting 
on what they would do if faced with a similar disaster.
Extension activities 
Make a class collage of pictures from Pompeii showing 
structures, artefacts and plaster casts. Find them on the 
internet or in textbooks. Some websites allow you to go 
for a virtual walk around Pompeii. Students could also 
find out about Herculaneum, the other town buried by 
Vesuvius.
Develop an emergency plan for surviving different 
stages of a volcanic eruption, from early warnings to the 
final stages when there is little chance of escape.
Answers
Mount Vesuvius erupts 2 and 5, 3, 4, 1
Daily life in Pompeii  Her clothing suggests she may 
be poor or a slave. He tries to guard her face from the 
toxic gases. Maybe she is with her family; This is a slave’s 
room in the slave quarters section of the home. The seal 
on the ring shows that the slave is owned by Quintus 
Poppaeus. He is keeping the money purse close by and 
plans to stay safe in his bed until the danger passes; 
The gladiators train at this gladiator school. Their 
armour must have been kept in a room upstairs.

Teacher’s notes – Roman houses
Objectives
l To interpret diagrams and written information 
about Roman houses and use it to explain the 
daily life and habits of people in Ancient Rome 
l To compare differing living conditions between 
rich and poor Romans in the city and country
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that housing in any 
society varies between different classes and 
location, and is dependent on many factors,  
such as location, a person’s employment and  
their socio-economic status.
Background
A lot of building material stretching across the 
empire has survived from Roman times, mainly their 
buildings constructed of stone and tile. Houses, 
especially ones belonging to the wealthy, were so 
well built that almost complete remains of villas 
and even whole towns have been found. However, 
there is little evidence of the wooden huts or wattle 
and daub buildings, thought to have been used 
throughout this time by many common citizens. The 
divide between the rich and poor is clearly signalled 
by their housing conditions, both in the city 
where many people lived and in the neighbouring 
countryside.
Starter activity
Ask students to think about how houses for people 
living in Ancient Rome may be different to their own 
house or flat. Consider also any differences between 
the rich and the poor.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet ‘Living in Rome’ and Activity sheet 
‘Living in the country’ describe four Roman dwellings, 
introducing students to the differences in living 
between the rich and the poor, urban and rural. 
In the Activity sheets ‘Roman houses (1)’ and ‘Roman 
houses (2)’ students identify and label four housing 
styles, and then compare them. 
Extension activity
1   Students could write a paragraph comparing a rich 
and poor townhouse in Ancient Rome.
2  Students could write real-estate advertisements for 
Ancient Roman properties for sale or lease. They could 
make models of a Roman villa for a class display.
Answers
Living in Rome  1 atrium, domus, insula, peristyle, lares  
2 domus: spacious, cool, ground-level, airy, private insula: 
cramped, stuffy, multistorey, noisy, smelly,
Roman houses (1) 1 (clockwise) atrium, peristyle, 
mosaic tiles; city house 2 (clockwise) many rooms, slave 
quarters, storehouses; country house 3 (clockwise) 
windowless room, three storeys high, ground-level 
shop; city house 4 (clockwise) mud walls, thatched roof; 
country house.

53
© Chrissie Michaels and Blake Education, 2011
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Religion
Objectives
l To identify the twelve major gods of the  
Roman Pantheon 
l To describe how Roman contact with Greek 
culture led to the adoption of Greek gods and 
mythology, and to make a comparison.
l To identify and describe some of the religious 
festivals that marked the Roman calendar
l To use examples from the festival calendar 
to gain an understanding of the importance 
of religion in the everyday life of the Roman 
people.
Prior knowledge
Students should have some appreciation of the 
role religion plays in many people’s life. They 
should know that not all religions are monotheistic, 
and that in the past people looked to religion 
rather than to science for explanations and 
understanding of the world around them.
Background
Etruscan admiration of Greek culture led to early 
Romans taking over the worship of Greek gods and 
goddesses for themselves. The Roman Pantheon 
had 12 major gods called the Dii Consentes. Romans 
changed the names of most gods (not Apollo) but 
kept the stories that went with them. 
Religion was considered very important to the 
survival of the Roman nation, with public worship 
highly regulated through the many religious 
festivals that took place almost every week of the 
year. The Pontifex Maximus, elected by the people, 
oversaw the religious laws and drew up the festival 
calendar. 
Starter activity
Ask students why they think many people believe 
in gods. Introduce the idea of mythology and 
religious stories that explain nature or aspects of the 
social world. Why do students think religion is still 
important to many people in our modern world? 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet ‘Family tree of early Roman gods’ 
introduces students to the Roman Pantheon. 
The Activity sheet ‘The Dii Consentes’ helps them to 
identify 12 major Roman gods, their associated symbols 
and responsibilities, and their Greek counterparts. 
The Activity sheet ‘A god for every purpose’ 
reinforces students’ understanding of the worship of 
many gods in Roman daily life. 
The Resource sheet ‘Calendar of religious festivals’ 
introduces students to some of the religious festivals of 
Rome, and the Activity sheet ‘Religious festivals, beliefs 
and daily life’ encourages them to think about how 
these related to the realities of Roman life. 
Extension activities
Students could research other myths about Roman 
gods and explore what they tell us about Roman 
beliefs and understandings of their world. They could 
try writing their own myths to explain an aspect of 
the modern world. 
Use the internet or textbooks to find pictures of 
Roman statues, temples, floor tiles or paintings showing 
the 12 Roman gods that made up the Dii Consentes. 
Make a collage of the pictures you find and label them 
with the gods’ names. 
Answers 
The Dii Consentes Jupiter, Juno, god of war, goddess of 
love, Minerva, goddess of the moon, childbirth and the 
hunt, god of the sea, Mercury, Ceres, god of the home 
and hearth, Vulcan, god of the sun, music and healing.
A god for every purpose Mercury, Minerva, Ceres, Vesta, 
Venus.
Religious festivals, beliefs and daily life Furrinalia, 
Fontinalia, ensure water supply; Lupercalia, celebrate 
fertility; Mindus, keep on the good side of the 
underworld spirits; Meditrinalia, to ensure good 
health; Saturnalia, recognition of reliance on slaves 
and honouring family life; Lares, honour the gods who 
guard households and give strength to the army.

Teacher’s notes – The great road builders
Objectives
l To gain an understanding that Romans were 
great road builders
l To identify and describe how and why Romans 
linked the known ancient world through their 
road network
l To draw conclusions about the significance  
and legacy of the Roman road system 
Prior knowledge
Students should bring to this unit a basic 
awareness of the importance of a road system  
as a transport and communication network.
Background
Ancient Romans were able to build an extraordinary 
network of roads in the known ancient world. Their 
straight and direct routes brought trade, improved 
social conditions and prosperity to many people 
in and outside of Rome. Such a great achievement 
came about through a combination of immense 
creativity and innovation (through designs and 
invention), as well as a well-organised, highly trained 
industry of ‘forced’ labour (army and slavery). The 
legacy left for future generations is still apparent, 
with some roads and many routes still in use today.
Starter activity
Ask the following questions to get students thinking 
about how roads affect the way we organise our 
society. Why are roads important? Why do we build 
freeways? What do road builders have to consider 
when making a road (direct route, road safety, 
effect on natural landscapes)? What equipment 
and machinery do we use?
Resource and activity sheets
The Activity sheet ‘The Appian Way opens’ introduces 
students to Rome’s first major road achievement. They 
learn about Roman technology in the Activity sheet 
‘Master road builders’.
In the Activity sheet ‘All roads lead to Rome’ students 
use a map to locate the expansion of the road system 
during the empire, before reflecting on Rome’s motives 
for developing such a network. 
The Activity sheet ‘Remarkable Roman road facts’ 
provides students with further information for them  
to interpret. 
The cloze activity on the Activity sheet ‘Great 
builders’ is a summary of the unit.
Extension activity
You can still travel along the Via Appia today. Students 
could use the internet to find some recent photos of 
it and write captions about the road’s use through the 
ages. They could imagine how it might look 2320 years 
from now.
Answers
Master road builders 1 camber – a gentle curve over 
the width of the road allows water to drain away; road 
hardener – a mixture of volcanic ash, lime, gravel and 
water that sets hard; groma – surveyor’s tool, sights out 
a straight line or sets lines at right angles. 2 chorobate – 
spirit level; camber – camber; road hardener – concrete.
All roads lead to Rome 2 England, Scotland, Egypt, 
Spain, Iraq 3 Fast movement of army; Communication 
network; Power from the top; A more prosperous 
empire; Imports to Rome; Wealth for Rome.
Remarkable Roman road facts 1 Thumbs up; 2 Thumbs 
down; 3 Thumbs up; 4 Thumbs down; 5 Thumbs up;  
6 Thumbs down
Great builders 1 builders, invented, tools, well-paved, 
empire, surveyors, peace, travel; business, routes, 
inventions; Extra word: ancient  2 False;  3 False;  4 True

Origins of Rome (1)
Material evidence suggests that people settled in Italy  
as early as 200 000 years ago. Archaeologists have found flint axes 
and, near Rome, Neanderthal skulls. This evidence suggests to 
historians that the early inhabitants lived short, nomadic lives.
The Etruscans, Sabines and Latins were groups of people who settled in the area near 
where Rome would begin. The main hills near the River Tiber are known as  
the Seven Hills. Modern historians believe that tribes settled down in the area some  
time before 1200 BCE. These groups of people built huts on the Seven Hills, where it was 
easier to defend themselves.
+  Consider the map above then answer the following questions in your workbook. 
 
1   Why you think so many tribes chose to settle in the Seven Hills area? 
 
2   What advantage did the hills and river provide?

Origins of Rome (2)
Over time the villages on the Seven Hills grew. The people drained the marshlands 
that had kept them apart and set up markets. The River Tiber became a busy route for 
trade. Because the Palatine Hill was near the lowest crossing point of the river it had 
the strongest position, and the village located there became the main city of Rome. 
Modern historians believe that Rome became a city around 753 BCE.
Material evidence
Material evidence is any object that helps us to understand the past. The discovery 
of small funeral urns on the Palatine Hill suggests that the people who lived there 
burned their dead. Archaeologists know that the Latins and Sabines used this practice. 
In contrast, the Etruscans buried their dead in huge tombs shaped like houses. 
The presence of funeral urns on Palatine Hill has led some historians to believe that  
the Latins and Sabines were Rome’s first townspeople.
+ 1    Underline in blue the sentence that tells why the Palatine Hill was chosen as the 
main site for Rome.
+ 2    Underline in red the sentence that tells us who some historians believe were 
most likely Rome’s first townspeople.

Etruscan tomb

Activity sheet – The foundations of Rome
The legend of Romulus and Remus
A legend is a story passed down from earlier times, which often mixes fact with fiction. 
The Roman historian Livy made the beginning of Rome sound exciting, romantic and 
powerful in the following story, which became a legend. 
Romulus and Remus
Twin boys called Romulus and Remus were born to Mars, the Roman god of war, 
and the daughter of a king. The twins’ wicked uncle wanted no threats to the 
throne, so he left the twins by the River Tiber to die. A she-wolf found the boys 
and cared for them, until a shepherd rescued and raised them. When they grew 
up, the brothers discovered who they really were.
As princes, they had many followers and they each chose to live on different hills – 
Romulus on the Palatine Hill, Remus on the Aventine Hill. Each brother wanted to 
build a city on his own hill. They quarrelled and during the fight Remus died.
Romulus named his new city Rome and became its first king in 753 BCE. But he 
needed people to live in his city, so he let slaves and criminals live there and stole 
women from the Sabine people, who lived in a nearby area. The Sabines declared 
war on Rome, but after a long battle, they agreed to join the kingdom of Romulus. 
At the end of Romulus’ life, Mars carried his son to the heavens, where he became 
a god called Quirinus.

Resource sheet – Roman society 
The Senate
 
● The Romans were ruled by kings from around 753 BCE to 510 BCE. Rome’s citizens 
did not want one person to have all the power, so they set up a new government, the 
Roman Republic, which lasted for over 400 years. 
 
● The Roman Republic was governed by a group of people called the Senate. The most 
powerful men of Rome formed the Senate and were called Senators. They all had 
duties and jobs in the government, such as leading the army, looking after finances, 
being a judge or protecting citizens’ rights.
 
● Two elected consuls from the Senate were the rulers of Rome. They ruled for only one 
year each. Then they had to wait 10 years for another turn. During this time they retired 
and served as pro-consuls (governors) of other provinces (places ruled by Rome). 
 
● Roman society at this time had two social classes of people: patricians and plebeians. 
Women, slaves and people from other places had no citizenship or voting rights.

Resource sheet – Roman society
Patricians
My family has been wealthy as long as we can remember. My grandfather says 
we can trace our noble family line back to the time of the kings. Grandfather is 
our pater familias (head of the household) because he is the oldest male in our 
family. Mother insists she has authority (power) over the home but she is really 
only in charge of the household slaves. Girls don’t have much power.
Tonight we are holding a feast to celebrate my father being voted into the 
Senate as a quaestor (financial advisor). Members of all the leading noble 
families will dine with us. They are mostly Senators. 
My father has been a patron to some wealthy tradespeople, giving them 
huge support and favours. They are also attending our feast tonight. My father 
says they are welcome here because Rome rewards hard work and ambition, 
but we have organised inferior (lower quality) food and wine for them, because 
of their lower status. Grandfather forbids them to be in the same room as him. 
He says they are ‘plebeian upstarts’. Birth is important to grandfather. When I am 
older, he will only allow me to marry a patrician and not a plebeian, even though 
the law says I can.
Tonight mother is going to wear all her finest jewellery. She has ordered the 
slaves to polish our beautiful mosaic tiled floors. The slaves are madly preparing 
nine courses of food. It’s so boring having to wait until the poison taster has 
tried them all to see if they are safe for me to eat! 
–  Fortuna, daughter in the house of Lucius Domitius Maximus

Resource sheet – Roman society 
Plebeians
We are a hardworking family. Father says we can hold our heads high, even if 
our tunics are plain and we live in a small flat. My father may only be a plebeian 
but he is a proud citizen of Rome. When I am older I, too, will become a citizen 
of Rome. I am sorry for mother and my sisters because they can never have 
citizenship, even though they are all free-born. 
Father is our pater familias, the head of our household. He is a baker and 
works in the shop on the ground floor below our flat. I am a hard worker like my 
father and help him for long hours in the bakery. Father says before he dies he 
will own many slaves who will build a grand tomb for him.  
My stomach is full from my breakfast of bread dipped in water. Mother even 
let me sprinkle raisins on the bread. I wondered why she was giving me such a 
treat and wearing her best jewellery made of painted clay.
‘Have you forgotten?’ she said, ‘Today is the festival (celebration) of Mars and 
Minerva. Later, we are to go to the Forum to see a juggler, just like the patricians 
will be doing!’
First she sends me off to collect some water from the public fountain. 
Rome is a wonderful city. We can go to religious festivals, go to the Forum, 
even see gladiators fight at the amphitheatre. Who cares if the patricians get  
the best seats in the stadium! 
–  Sebasta, son of the baker Drusus

During the time of the Roman Republic (   ) Gaius Julius

Caesar was away fighting in Gaul, there were riots back in Rome.

Caesar’s army crossed the Rubicon (   ), and returned to 
Italy to start a war against Pompey. Caesar won the battle, 
and Pompey fled to Greece. Caesar was named ‘dictator’. He 
followed Pompey to Greece and defeated him. Pompey fled  
to Egypt, where he was killed by the Egyptians. Caesar’s power 
was now unchallenged (   ), and the Senate feared that he 
wanted too much power for himself. 
During his rule, Caesar forgave many of his former enemies. He passed fairer tax 
reforms and laws. He introduced a 12-month calendar. The month Iulius (  ) was named 
after him. He had new buildings built in Rome. 
By 44 BCE he had filled the Senate with supporters, who gave him the title ‘dictator for 
life’ – a life that was soon to be cut short by murder.

Caesar’s murder
Julius Caesar was murdered on 15 March 44 BCE by a group of Senators who felt he held 
too much power. The night he was murdered, Caesar dismissed his bodyguards. Some 
people believe this shows he was overconfident.
An old friend of Caesar’s, Marcus Junius Brutus, was one of the Senators who took part 
in the murder. According to the Roman historian Suetonius, ‘Et tu, Brut, fili?’ were the words 
spoken in Latin (the language spoken by Romans) by Julius Caesar on being stabbed by 
Brutus. This means ‘And you, Brutus, son?’ in English. Caesar felt betrayed that Brutus was 
among his killers.
The other senators and I,

to dispose of Julius Caesar, although we once  
called him ‘friend’. His wish to rule alone is against  
what our Roman Republic stands for. On this day,  
the Ides of March, we shall corner him at the  
Theatre of Pompey as he comes to meet  
the Senate. People of Rome, we are  
once again free …’

The main fighting unit of the Roman army was the legion. Each legion had about 5000 to 
6000 soldiers, called legionaries. The legionaries formed strong, disciplined units. Their 
commanding officer was called a legate. 
On average during the Roman Empire, there were about 30 legions. At its largest, the 
Roman army had over 500 000 legionaries. The legions were so well organised and well 
trained that the army became almost unstoppable.

Free-born citizens
Ancient Romans did not believe that everyone had equal rights. The biggest difference 
between people was whether they were free or slaves. Men who were born free were 
called free-born citizens. No women were citizens. Women had few legal rights and were 
not allowed to vote. 
Free-born citizens could:
+  1   Which of the above would you most value if you were a free-born Roman citizen.
Clothing
 
● Only free-born male citizens could wear a 
toga (a long, semi-circular cloak). Until he 
was 16, a free-born boy wore a toga with a 
purple stripe. 
 
● Plebeian (ordinary class) men wore a plain 
white toga virilis (toga of manhood). 
 
● Patrician (noble class) men wore one with  
a stripe. 
 
● Free-born women wore a stola (floor-length 
dress), which covered their under-tunic. 
Not all the people who lived in Rome were free-born citizens. Roman law allowed 
anyone to come and live in the city, but they had to support themselves. Later, people 
across the Roman Empire could buy Roman citizenship. Freedmen and freedwomen 
were people who had been set free from slavery, but they had fewer rights than free-born 
citizens. Again, men had more rights than women. 
 
●choose their own work
 
●marry
 
●travel from one place to another
 
●vote for the government 
 
● receive some free food from the 
government
 
●go to the gladiator games
 
●go to the public baths
 
●have lots of free time
 
●be protected by law.

Slaves
In Ancient Rome, people did not believe that everyone was equal. Almost everyone 
accepted the use of slaves. Slaves were owned by other people and had no rights.  
They worked for little or no reward. A slave might be: 
 
●a criminal who committed a serious crime
 
●a prisoner taken in war
 
●a person from another land who was kidnapped and sold by slave traders 
 
●a poor person who sold himself or herself into slavery
 
●a child born to slaves.
The use of slaves helped Rome become wealthy. Slaves did a lot of work for a very low 
cost. They carried out all the farming to produce food or goods. Slaves that could read and 
write (often Greeks) became doctors or scribes. Many gladiators were slaves. Slaves lived 
with the families that owned them. One senator had over 4000 slaves. 
Slaves wore simple clothes. Sometimes their owners made them wear a type of 
uniform. Some were branded, or wore a tag with their owner’s name on it in case they 
escaped.
Saturnalia (a mid-winter festival) ended 
with a slave’s holiday. A kind slave owner 
would wait on the family’s slaves and 
serve them a special feast on this day.

Resource sheet – Gladiators
Gladiator combat
The word gladiator means swordsman. It 
comes from the Latin word for sword: gladius. 
Most gladiators were prisoners of war, slaves or 
condemned criminals. They were expected to 
fight to the death in bloody combat against:
 
●other gladiators
 
●other criminals, slaves or prisoners of war
 
● people Romans considered to be a threat 
(for example, Christians and Jews) 
 
 
 
The Colosseum
 
●wild animals. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
Arena is Latin for sand. An arena was a place filled with sand to soak up the blood 
spills. After each contest the arena was freshly raked. Later, slaves built bigger arenas, or 
amphitheatres, to house the growing crowds. The Flavian Amphitheatre was also called 
the Colosseum. With room for over 250 000 people, it was the largest arena, built in the 
middle of Rome. The ruins of the Colosseum are now a popular tourist attraction.
 
● The first gladiator match was set up in a cattle market to honour a man who had 
just died. 
 
● Then it became common for gladiators to fight at funeral games or to honour the 
gods in public spaces, such as market squares. 
 
● As time went on, gladiators fought in arenas, to please the emperor and entertain 
the huge crowds who came to watch them. 
 
● Gladiator events were often held on public holidays, when gladiators fought to the 
death to honour their gods. 
 
●A morning contest might be animal fights, or people versus big cats. 
 
●During lunch came clowns and public executions. 
 
●Sometimes the arena was flooded for spectacular sea battles. 
 
● Single combat events between popular gladiators took place as main events, or 
over many days of gladiator game, such as the Colosseum games in 100 CE.
 
● After hundreds of years, Emperor Honorius decides that gladiator combat is too 
cruel and stops it. The Colosseum closes.

Gladiator FAQ
How do we know about gladiators? 
Ancient Roman pictures of gladiators still exist today. Some are on mosaic tiles.  
Others are carvings or paintings. 
Could women be gladiators?
Yes. Most of the discoveries show gladiators were male. However, one stone tablet  
shows two female gladiators fighting with daggers. The Roman poet, Juvenal, left  
a nasty poem about women gladiators, saying they were a disgrace!
Were there many different types of gladiators?
Yes. Two examples were the secutor, who 
was heavily armed, and the retiarius, a  
net-fighter who wore little armour and  
relied on being fit and fast. 
What happened to a wounded gladiator?
When the crowd pointed their thumbs  
down at a wounded gladiator, this meant  
‘no mercy’. Some slaves came out into the arena  
dressed in masks. One carried a mallet (hammer) to strike the injured gladiator a final blow, 
while another slave dragged away the body. Lucky gladiators lived to fight another day.

Resource sheet – Pompeii
Pompeii is buried
Around noon on 24 August 79 CE, a loud bang came from Mount Vesuvius. A spout of dark 
ash rose up from the mountain. It formed a thick cloud, blotting out the sun and blowing 
towards the south. Day instantly turned to night.
 
● For nineteen hours, pyroclastic material (ash, pumice and gases) rained onto the 
coastal town of Pompeii, 10 kilometres away from the volcano. 
 
● Modern experts estimate that 2000 out of the town’s 20 000 inhabitants stayed, 
while others fled. Intense heat overpowered the people who remained behind. 
Deadly gases choked them.
 
● The mountain dome collapsed, and the town was completely buried by ash. 
Everything – humans, animals, buildings and objects – was covered.
 
● For nearly 1700 years, Pompeii remained hidden. Archaeologists began excavating 
Pompeii in 1748, but scientific records were only kept from 1864. So far, 60 per cent 
of the town has been recovered. 
 
● This was not the first time 
disaster struck Pompeii. At the 
time Vesuvius erupted, many 
buildings still lay in ruins or were 
under repair from an earthquake 
17 years earlier.
 
● Before the eruption, Pompeii 
was 500 metres from the sea. 
Volcanic ash and rubble filled 
the bay. Now, it is two kilometres 
inland. Today the ruins are a  
vast, open-air museum visited  
by tourists from all around  
the world.
Roman graffiti can still be seen on the 
walls at Pompeii.

A personal view of Pompeii
Pliny the Younger lived from 61 to 112 CE. As a teenager, Pliny lived by the Bay of  
Naples with his uncle. He witnessed the disaster hitting Pompeii from a distance.  
While his uncle sailed across the bay to help with the rescue efforts, Pliny remained 
behind. Sadly, Pliny’s uncle did not survive. Afterwards, survivors told Pliny about what his 
uncle would have experienced there.
Pliny went on to become a Roman official. He wrote many letters. These were compiled 
into ten books. In one of these letters, he wrote about the disaster at Pompeii.
A volcanic eruption with huge columns of gases and ash is known as a Plinian eruption.  
It was named after Pliny because he was the first person to describe it. 
+   1    Imagine that you are on board one of the ships that sail across the Bay of Naples 
to rescue the residents of Pompeii. Your ship remains at sea, unable to land. In 
your workbook, describe what you see, hear, smell and taste in the air. How do 
you feel when you realise you can’t rescue anyone? What do you say to others 
upon your return?
Elsewhere there was daylight,  
but my uncle and his friends were in darkness.
It was much blacker than any normal night. 
After lighting torches and lamps, they ran down 
onto the beach to see if there was any chance of 
escape by boat, but the sea was too rough …
Broad sheets of fire and leaping flames glared 
through the darkness.

Pompeii casts
During the destruction at Pompeii, people were fully clothed as they tried to flee. Many 
choked from toxic gases and their bodies were soon covered by dust, ash and rocks. The 
pyroclastic material hardened into rock around the victims. Their bodies decomposed, 
leaving spaces in the rock.
In 1863 CE, Giuseppe Fiorelli 
was the director of excavations at 
Pompeii. He worked out a method for 
reconstructing the features of people, 
animals and objects that were buried. 
He made casts (plaster moulds) of the 
hollow spaces left in the hard rock.
Most of the people in Pompeii died 
very quickly. However, most of the 
casts for the Pompeii victims make it 
look like they died in agony. Experts 
know that this was really because their 
muscles contracted in the heat after 
they died.
Modern casts are still being made in 
Pompeii, but from harder substances. 
Experts have made a cast of a woman’s 
body found in the ruins of Oplontis, 
near Torre Annunziata. This cast, made 
from glass fibre, shows her skeleton, 
along with some of the jewels she wore.
+  1    In what way has the invention of making casts added to our understanding of

Living in Rome
My family’s walled domus has twelve  
rooms. Our study, office, bedrooms and kitchen  
are built around a cool atrium hall. The atrium has no  
roof, it is open to the sky, so we can catch rainwater in the  
pool below. Our garden is called a peristyle. It has a fountain 
and pool to cool the hot summer air. Our slaves have their  
own area. There are small shops at the front, which  
we rent to others. A front door opens  
onto the street.
I carry food and water buckets  
up the six flights of stairs to our insula.  
The rooms of the insula are small and many  
people live in the building. There are no windows  
and on these hot days I can hardly breathe. I must 
burn my oil lamp all day. There are always house  
fires in Rome. Day and night are so noisy, wagons  
roll by and workers call out from their ground 
 floor shops … The smells are disgusting!  
But I must not complain, or our  
lares will be angry.

Calendar of religious festivals 
The Pontifex Maximus (pon-tuh-feks max-i-mus) was the religious leader voted in by 
the people. He drew up a calendar of religious festivals so people could honour the gods 
and goddesses.
January 
Festival of Agonalia
January 1 and 5
Figs, dates and honey are 
offered to Janos, god of doors. 
Family members receive 
gifts of fruit and money.
Romans prayed to Janos  
for advice as he was the 
god of doors, beginnings 
and endings.
February
Lupercalia 
Celebrates love and fertility. 
Honours Faunus, god of 
nature and fertility, and 
Lupercus, god of shepherds.
March
Lares
Teams of 12 men run 
through the streets in 
body armour to honour 
the Lares, gods who guard 
households. 
Soldiers will soon begin 
fighting again. They do not 
fight in winter.
April
On April 1, Ancient Romans 
believe the Mindus, the 
passage to the underworld, 
opens to allow the spirits of 
the dead to roam freely.
May
Ambarvalia 
The gods Ceres and Dea Dia 
bless the growing of plants. 
Also on May 15, people 
make animal sacrifices to 
honour the River Tiber.
June
Lesser Quinquatrus 
Flute players who play 
at religious ceremonies 
celebrate this three-day 
festival in honour of 
Minerva.
July
Furrinalia
Honours the goddess 
Furrina. Celebrates 
those who search for 
underground water sources.
August
Consualia
Held for the god of grain, 
Consus. Flowers are draped 
around the necks of 
working horses and oxen. 
They are rested from work.
September
Meditrinalia
Offerings of fruit are given 
to Meditrina, the goddess  
of medicine.
October
Fontinalia
Flowers are thrown into the 
springs and wells to honour 
Fons, god of the water 
source.
November
Ludi Plebeii 
These plebeian games 
honour Jupiter. After a 
procession from the Forum 
to the Circus Maximus, the 
common people enjoy 
theatre and athletic events.
December
Saturnalia
Kind owners serve their 
slaves a special meal and 
give them a day off (on 
December 25) during 
this mid-winter festival 
in honour of Saturn.

Activity sheet – The great road builders
Via Appia opens 
The Senate today put on games at 
the local amphitheatre to celebrate 
the opening of its first major link 
road, the Via Appia. Linking 
Rome to Brundisium on the 
south-east coast, this direct road 
is great news for the Republic. Not 
only will our troops better defend 
our coast, but also the road opens 
up a faster route for our many 
Greek friends who already visit 
this glorious city. 
Leading engineer Dio Commodus 
Cassius says the surface will last 
for a long time. ‘We have used four 
layers, about a metre deep from top 
to bottom. A chalk and sand base 
is tightly packed with big stones. 
A layer of paving stones tops sand, 
gravel and broken bricks.’ 
Cassius adds, ‘To make the 
foundation even firmer we used a 
new hardener. Volcanic ash, lime, 
bits of gravel and broken rock mix 
with water and set hard. The road 
is also higher in the middle due 
to a camber, which curves down 
into drains on either side.’
He promises that not even 
Apollo’s four-horse chariot will 
get stuck in the mud on this road. 
Hail to our sun God as he crosses 
the sky to give light to Rome! 
Cassius gives glowing praise to 
his team. ‘We owe them a lot. 
Equipment such as the groma 
helps us to measure out land and 
lay out a straight road, while the 
chorobate is a great way to level 
the surface. Soldiers and slaves 
have also done a top building job.’ 
He rejects concerns about traveller 
safety. ‘Bah! No harm will come 
to anyone! We already have slaves 
building mansiones along the 
road where users can have a brief 
rest or meal, even stay overnight 
if they wish. A great boom for the 
traders too!’ 
He says there is much excitement 
in the Republic about future road 
plans. ‘One day, we plan to be the 
master road builder of the known 
world.’ 
312 BCE 
The Appian Way opens

ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
5
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – The Industrial Revolution in Britain
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge for this unit.
Background
Many of the key features of the Middle Ages continued 
past the period of the Medieval era (approximately 
700 CE to 1400 CE). Most people lived on farms or 
worked on large estates for the wealthy elite. Moving 
between social classes was almost impossible, as those 
from the lower classes generally had little access to 
education or money and could not interact or compete 
successfully with those who inherited their wealth and 
power. 
Over time, social changes began to challenge these 
expected ways of living. There was a rapid population 
growth in the 1800s: from 8 million people in 1801 to 
26 million people in 1881. This was because people 
continued to have large families while improvements 
in medicines, sanitation and drinking water (later half 
of 19th century), and the quality of food reduced the 
mortality rate. 
Increasing numbers of people could not remain on 
the farms where they had traditionally lived because 
agricultural inventions meant their labour was 
unnecessary. They were forced to move to cities to look 
for jobs. Factory owners could then hire large numbers 
of people as unskilled labourers and so increase their 
production to meet the increasing need for material 
goods demanded by the newly established middle 
class. This led to a demand for improved transport to 
source raw materials from other countries (usually 
colonies) and send the finished products from factories 
in Britain to other parts of the country and overseas.
Starter activity
Show a video or series of images to introduce life in the 
industrial period. 
Useful documentaries include:
• Tony Robinson’s Worst Jobs in History, 
Episode: Industrial Jobs
• The Supersizers Go ..., Episode: Victorian, BBC
Brainstorm with the students what you found out 
about life in the industrial period.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Map of the British Empire’, asks 
students to use a map to identify the locations of key 
industrial countries and British colonies. Students will 
use a colour key to identify the trade sources of raw 
products.
The Activity sheet, ‘Technology and transport’, lists 
some key technological events for students to show on 
a timeline. As an additional activity, students are asked 
to research three more key events and add them to the 
timeline.
In the Activity sheet, ‘Causes of the Industrial 
Revolution’, students highlight key terms in a list of 
causes of the Industrial Revolution, organised into 
themes of agriculture, factories, people and transport. 
Students then compile a glossary of unfamiliar terms. 
In the final Activity sheet, ‘Essay plan’, students are 
guided through the process of creating an essay 
plan using the information from the Resource sheet, 
‘Causes of the Industrial Revolution’. Discuss the TEEEM 
structure with the class, especially if students have not 
used it before. As an extension activity, students are 
asked to use their plan to write an essay.
TEEEM Paragraph Plan 
Always start with a topic sentence and always end with 
a mini-conclusion. Put the evidence, explanation and 
essay keywords in the middle in whatever order you 
like. 
•  T – Topic sentence: introduce your specific topic
•  E – Evidence: to support your ideas
•  E – Explain: your ideas in your own words
•   E – Essay keywords: use keywords from the essay 
question and the topic sentence to show you are 
answering the question
•   Mini-conclusion: sum up what you said in that 
paragraph.
Extension ideas
Students could work individually or in small groups to 
research a different cause of the Industrial Revolution. 
Have them use what they find out to create an 
extended response, poster, video or ICT presentation.
Objectives
• Learn about the nature of the Industrial 
Revolution
• Identify key events that led to the Industrial 
Revolution
• Explore the trading relationships of countries

Achieve!
ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
12
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Factories
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution.
Background
The Industrial Revolution can be considered to have 
begun with inventors who wanted to make products 
faster and easier. Technological developments were 
often resisted by the local skilled workers. The workers 
tried to sabotage the new machines and attack the 
inventors because skilled labour would no longer be 
needed to make quality products. These workers were 
trying to protect their livelihoods. 
Wealthy people often valued these new inventions 
because they made it possible to start factories. With 
these new machines and cheap unskilled labour, many 
products could be made at a discounted price, and 
then sold for a good profit. Many middle class and 
upper class people could now afford to buy these 
new factory products. But the lives of the lower class 
became far more difficult and precarious. Working 
in factories and coal mines was dangerous, dirty and 
unhealthy work. Many laboured for long hours for six 
or seven days each week. If they had a day off, it was 
usually on Sunday and they were expected to attend 
church. Family life became more complicated as 
children often had to work in the factories from a very 
young age to help support the family. 
In response, many men banded together to protect 
their working rights in the new trade unions. These 
trade unions took longer to become successful in 
places like England where the class system was 
entrenched. However, Australia was often described 
as a ‘working man’s paradise’ and moved quickly to 
adopt trade unions. They became a usual part of the 
Australian working experience and, later, political 
experience.
Starter activity
Show students images of inventions from the Industrial 
Revolution, such as the spinning jenny, cotton gin, 
sewing machine, telegraph and steam engine. 
Ask questions about the images and have students 
give reasons for their answers. 
• What do they look like?
• What might they do? How do you know?
• Why might they be important in that time? 
Repeat the activity with images of factory and coal 
workers from the same period. 
• How do you think they live?
• What were their living conditions probably like?
Discuss as a group what these images tell us about the 
Industrial Revolution.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Textiles workers’, provides an 
overview of the impacts of inventions in the textiles 
industry. All people with a first and last name are real 
people, with text referring to their lives. Those people 
with initials as surnames are fictionalised characters 
whose dialogue is based on historical facts. Students 
will use this information to complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Continuity and change’, where they consider the 
positive and negative aspects of inventions.
The Activity sheet, ‘Coal mining’, explores mining 
developments. From this information and a primary 
source – the testimony of Betty Harris – students learn 
about the effects of these developments.
On the Activity sheet, ‘Factories’, students consider how 
factories affected cottage industries. They also explore 
the new working environments of factory workers. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Australian and British trade unions’, 
looks at the different experiences of workers fighting 
for their rights in Australia and Britain.
Extension ideas
Have students explore primary sources relating to the 
lives of workers. They should choose one source and 
analyse it in terms of what it tells them about everyday 
life in that time. Here are two useful websites:
•  http://www.victorianweb.org/history/workers1.html
•  http://www.historyteacher.net/APEuroCourse/
WebLinks/WebLinks-IndustrialRevolution.htm
Objectives
• Learn about key inventions in the industrial 
period
• Consider the impacts of these inventions on 
the development of factories and the lives of 
the workers
• Explore the rise of the trade union movement 
in response to the expansion of factories
Web addresses were functional at the time of 
publication but teachers should check them for 
inappropriate content and to ensure that they are 
still functional before use with students.

Achieve!
ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
18
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Transport
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution.
Background
In 1710, Thomas Newcomen constructed a steam 
engine that generated vertical energy (up and down 
movement). Newcomen used this engine to make 
pumps for deep pit mining to prevent flooding. In 
1764, James Watt realised that he could use Thomas 
Newcomen’s ideas to construct a steam engine that 
used rotary motion (circular motion). This meant that 
different types of machines and transport could be 
invented. George Stephenson used James Watt’s rotary 
steam engine as a source of energy for the first steam 
train. This steam engine was also used in other forms of 
transport such as steamships. 
In 1770, James Cook went looking for the mysterious 
southern land. He confirmed sightings of Australia 
and New Zealand. Britain used Australia in particular 
as a convict settlement from 1788. Australia gradually 
shifted from a country of punishment to a country of 
opportunity as settlers arrived and took up pastoral 
land. These new settlers objected to the convicts and 
in 1840, New South Wales banned transportation. 
However, transportation to Australia only ended in 
1868 when Western Australia received a final ship of 
convicts. Western Australia continued to be a penal 
settlement for some time after 1868, but received no 
further transports.
Starter activity
Discuss the modes of transport that students use. How 
does transport technology influence their everyday 
interactions with people and the places they go? How 
would their lives be affected if walking was their only 
mode of transport?
Interesting fact: Improvements in transportation in the 
Victorian period (1800s) moved the average distance 
of spouses from about 5 km away to 30 km away, as 
people no longer had to rely on walking to meet and 
woo someone.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Transportation’, identifies the 
improvements in transport in the 1800s with an 
emphasis on the railway system. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Railways in England and Australia’, 
compares the development of railway systems in these 
countries. Students copy and complete comprehension 
questions for each section.
Through the Activity sheet, ‘Clippers and steamships’, 
students explore the realities of ship travel. They also 
consider how they would feel, experiencing that 
journey.
The Activity sheet, ‘Convicts and crime’, explores 
the reasons for transportation to Australia, and the 
perspectives of different groups of people. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Settlers in Australia’, students 
consider different reasons for moving to Australia. 
Guide the class through analysing the primary source 
emigration poster through CHIPS: 
•  caption (What words are there on the poster? Why are 
they used?) 
• history (What events were happening then?) 
•  interrogate source (What do you find interesting or 
unusual about the poster?) 
•  people (What people and animals are included? How 
are they represented?)  
•  symbols (What signs or symbols are used? How do 
these persuade and encourage people?).
Extension ideas
•   Students could visit the website ‘Convict Records’ 
to explore the different reasons people were 
transported to Australia and the lengths of their 
sentences. Have them compare and contrast three 
different convicts.
    http://www.convictrecords.com.au/crimes
•   Students could also use the Victorian Railway website 
to chart the development of steam trains in Victoria 
from the 1850s to the 1900s.
     https://museumvictoria.com.au/railways/theme.
aspx?theme=448&lvl=1
Objectives
• Learn about new developments in transport
• Explore how new transportation affected the 
movement of people
• Understand why people moved to Australia

publication but teachers should check them for 
inappropriate content and to ensure that they are 
still functional before use with students.

Achieve!
ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
24
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Land
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution. 
Background
Before the Industrial Revolution, land was used the 
same way for centuries. During the Medieval period, 
farming land was organised by the village. They 
distributed land to the farmers and rotated it regularly 
so that people were not stuck with poor farm land all 
the time. In order to keep the land fertile, medieval 
farmers used the three-field system. This involved 
ploughing two fields and leaving one field fallow 
(unused) and then rotating fields each year for three 
years. 
During the Industrial Revolution, farming changed 
dramatically. New machinery meant less human 
labour was needed. The land was also fenced in due to 
‘enclosure laws’. This meant that the village no longer 
shared and rotated the land used by the farmers in the 
area. Instead, fields were owned by individuals. The 
owners of the rich, fertile fields grew richer and could 
buy more land. The owners of arid or infertile land 
became poorer. Many had to leave when they could no 
longer afford to own land.
Some people chose to move to Australia as settlers. 
Others were transported to Australia for committing 
crimes. Some of these crimes, such as ‘being homeless’ 
and ‘associating with bad people’, are not what we 
consider to be crimes today. 
Australia was a land rapidly changing from the natural 
to the developed as settlers took land from the 
Indigenous Australian peoples. They built cities and 
towns on the sites of regular Indigenous Australian 
camping locations. The names of the colonies of 
Australia changed regularly, reflecting these changing 
stages: 
• Indigenous Australian peoples and their culture 
• penal colonies
•  a nation of bush people with the first European 
settlers
• a place of impossible riches with the gold rush
• a working man’s paradise for the new working class
• a federated country
all within the industrial period.
Starter activity
Discuss how we use land today; for example, 
‘McMansions’, living in capital cities, multistorey 
apartment buildings. Then consider how land was used 
100 or 200 years ago; for example, smaller houses for 
larger families with gardens to grow food, more people 
living in rural areas. As a class, make a Venn diagram to 
show the similarities and differences.
Resource and Activity sheets
On the Activity sheet, ‘Advances in agriculture’, students 
complete a cloze activity to find out how the Industrial 
Revolution impacted on agricultural life. 
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Country or city’, 
students consider why people moved between 
the city and the country, and the advantages and 
disadvantages of each lifestyle.  
The Resource sheet, ‘The Pioneer’, has an image of 
Frederick McCubbin’s famous painting. Students use 
this image to complete the Activity sheet, ‘Landscapes 
of Australia’. Through analysing this painting they 
explore the changing view of Victoria from first 
settlement to a generation later.
The Activity sheet, ‘Changing Australia’, uses maps of 
Australia and its various colonies, states and territories 
to look at how European settlement of Australia 
changed over time. 
Extension activities
Provide maps, posters, paintings or photographs 
of your town or city from different time periods; 
for example, now, 50 years ago, 100 years ago and 
150 years ago. Websites such as http://trove.nla.gov.au, 
state libraries and local history groups may be useful in 
sourcing these images.  
Discuss with the class the changes over time shown by 
the images. 
Objectives
• Understand how the use of geographical 
regions changed over time
• Consider how land was used by different 
people and how that use affected population 
movements
• Analyse images to improve understanding of 
the historical time period

publication but teachers should check them for 
inappropriate content and to ensure that they are 
still functional before use with students.
