ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
30
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Women
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution.
Background
Women had long been seen as inferior to men. This 
was reinforced by the Catholic and later Protestant 
churches who held to the idea of all women being 
tainted by the ‘sins of Eve’. Women were generally 
prejudiced against, treated almost as children and 
forced to work largely within the household. The few 
women who could express themselves through culture, 
literature or politics have often been misrepresented or 
ignored by history. It is important to remember that the 
absence of women’s writing or cultural activities does 
not mean that women were not engaging in these 
activities. Rather, women’s activities were devalued, 
there were more restrictions on their involvement in 
such activities, and little effort made to preserve them. 
Issues such as marriage and divorce were highly 
significant for women. Once married, many women’s 
rights to property and possessions passed to their 
husbands. Married women could engage in few 
activities without their husband’s support or presence. 
In the 19th century, divorce laws were finally 
introduced in Britain and its colonies, including 
Australia. However, women were still prejudiced 
against in the causes for divorce. In the late 
19th century, women challenged this inequality by 
seeking political representation through the vote 
(suffrage) and the right to be members of parliament. 
These women were called suffragettes or suffragists. 
Starter activity
Talk to students about voting. You may want to discuss 
a recent election. Discuss why we vote and what 
impact it could have if groups in society were not 
allowed to vote. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The first two activity sheets look at suffragettes and 
their fight for the right of women to vote. The Activity 
sheet, ‘British suffragettes’, considers what women had 
to do to get the vote. The Activity sheet, ‘Australian 
suffragettes’, looks at when women obtained the right 
to vote in Australia. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Marriage and divorce laws’, explores 
the idea of allowed causes of divorces, and how this 
has changed over time. ‘Aggravated adultery’ meant 
that the husband had to be highly obvious about his 
adultery, or combine it with physical cruelty, two years’ 
desertion, bigamy, sodomy, bestiality, incest or rape in 
order to be divorced. Women could be divorced for a 
single act of adultery.
In the Activity sheet, ‘Writing women’, students learn 
about two significant female writers who championed 
equality in the 1800s.
The Activity sheet, ‘Caroline Chisholm’, provides 
in-depth information about Caroline Chisholm’s 
philanthropy in Australia.
Extension ideas
Watch one of the movie adaptations of Charlotte 
Bronte’s Jane Eyre to broaden the students’ 
understanding of women’s lives in the 1840s. The 
main character, Jane, was middle class. The way she 
was treated by servants and by the upper class (with 
the exception of how she is sometimes treated by 
Mr Rochester) fits with the experiences many middle 
class women would have at the time.
Objectives
• Gain a stronger understanding of the position 
of women during the Industrial Revolution
• Learn about female writers and how they 
influenced women’s rights
• Learn about a female inventor and consider her 
role in the Industrial Revolution

ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
36
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Men
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution. They will benefit from knowing 
what suffrage is and who suffragettes were.
Background
The position of men in society underwent significant 
changes during the Industrial Revolution. Previously, 
a man was unquestionably the head of his household. 
Often all members of a family worked, but it was the 
man’s skilled labour that brought in the most money. 
With the move from skilled labour to mechanisation 
brought by the Industrial Revolution, skilled males 
became less valuable. Factory owners wanted cheap 
labourers to work with the machines in their factories. 
Women and children were cheaper than men, so were 
hired more often. An increasing number of fit and 
able men became subject to the Poor Law restrictions 
because they were could not find jobs to support their 
families. 
The Chartist movements in Britain (1838–1858) 
brought about discussions of universal male suffrage. 
People no longer believed that only rich men who 
owned property deserved the right to vote and be 
represented in parliament. In the late 19th century, 
there was also the suffragette movement pushing 
for women to have the vote. This also challenged 
the male social identity as the dominant, intelligent, 
knowledgeable gender. The conflict between the 
traditional idea of the strong man and the actual social 
reality was problematic for many men.
Starter activity
Present the following wage information to the class. 
• 
 Men usually earned 10–15 shillings a week
• 
Women usually earned 5 shillings a week
• 
Children usually earned 1 shilling a week 
Have the students consider which worker would be 
seen as more valuable in these situations:
• 
 A factory owner who is keen to spend no more than 
100 shillings a week staffing his factory. 
• 
 A family (mother, father and three children) who 
need to pay rent at approximately 5 shillings a 
month. 
Discuss the conflict between the needs of families and 
the needs of factory owners.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘The Poor Laws’, explores changes in 
the way that poor people were provided for. Students 
copy and complete comprehension questions for each 
section.
The Resource sheet, ‘Society’s expectations’, identifies  
differences between social expectations of men 
and the reality of men’s experiences. Students use 
this information to complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Expectations versus reality’, by writing third person and 
first person perspectives on how men lived. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Chartists’, discusses the movement 
that pushed for all men, including those who were 
poor, to have a say in how the country was governed. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Questioning voting’, students 
are guided through the process of writing complex 
questions about the Chartist movement. Then they 
choose one of these questions to answer. 
Extension activities
Have students research a famous Australian man 
who lived in the 1800s. Suggestions: Henry Lawson, 
Barcroft Henry Boake, Ned Kelly, Frederick McCubbin, 
Banjo Patterson, Edmund Barton, Alfred Deakin. 
Ask students to identify the ways this man fits what 
society expected of men at the time; for example, 
being the breadwinner, heterosexual, head of the 
house, married, strong and emotionless. Also identify 
the ways in which he did not fit this expected role; 
for example, being homosexual, intellectual, a carer, 
emotional or supported financially by a partner. 
Objectives
• Understand the social concept of masculinity
• Identify how the position of men changed 
during the Industrial Revolution
• Consider the importance of all men having the 
right to vote

ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
42
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Children
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution. An understanding of the factory 
system may be useful for understanding child labour.
Background
The position of children in Victorian society changed 
over time. At first, they were often seen as additional 
labour within the family. Most people lived on farms 
and having many children who could all work was 
valuable. However, there was less need for large 
families as people moved away from farms or became 
tenant farmers. At the time, people could not plan or 
restrict pregnancies so the population continued to 
grow. From a young age, children were often employed 
in factories or mines to supplement their parents’ 
wages. Sometimes it was easier for children to get jobs 
because they were cheaper to hire. 
When parents were employed and children weren’t, 
there were concerns about who would look after 
the children. Some families could rely on relatives or 
friends. However, many children were left to fend for 
themselves during the day, or at night if their parents 
worked night shifts. 
Governments in Britain and Australia decided that 
education might prevent these independent and 
unmonitored children from joining criminal gangs. 
They began developing education departments and 
systems to meet this need. 
Starter activity
Watch the documentary The Children who built 
Victorian Britain, BBC, 2007. It has good descriptions 
of the experiences of children during the Industrial 
Revolution. It’s great to watch by itself or you could 
pause it at regular intervals for students to take notes.  
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Education’, looks at the introduction 
of the education system in Australia and Britain. 
Students complete the information by crossing out the 
incorrect word in each set of brackets. Then students 
use that information to complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Education for all?’. Here, they consider the perspectives 
of different groups on aspects of education. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Child labourers’, provides students 
with an understanding of life as a child labourer in the 
industrial period. They use this information to complete 
the Activity sheet, ‘Plan a story’, where they plan a story 
about children during the industrial period.  
Extension activities
• 
 Work with the students to compile a table 
comparing children’s lives in modern times to 
children’s lives in the industrial period. You could 
include aspects such as education, housing, work, 
family life and ages for specific activities such as 
marriage and voting. 
• 
 Have students write a paragraph outlining what 
they appreciate most about today’s lifestyle.
• 
 As a class, read a passage from Oliver Twist by 
Charles Dickens (1812–1870). It is about a poor boy 
who lives in a workhouse and is then sold into a 
parish apprenticeship. Students may find Dickens’ 
language inaccessible; there are many movie 
adaptations available.
Objectives
• Understand the unique perspective of children 
during the Industrial Revolution
• Consider different perspectives on the same 
situation
• Use empathy to help create a narrative that 
demonstrates historical knowledge

ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
47
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Different groups in society
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution.
Background
Racism was a significant element of society in the 
1800s. These xenophobic attitudes were connected to a 
newly developed sense of nationalism. This meant that 
a country was becoming more than the place you lived 
– it was an emblematic symbol of your identity. This led 
to an easy acceptance of imperialist attitudes in which 
the country controlling an Empire, such as Britain, 
valued themselves and their abilities over those of the 
people in the colonies they invaded and controlled. 
Imperial European countries and their cultures were 
more valuable than those of other countries.
In colonies such as Australia, these racist attitudes 
were expressed through the treatment of Indigenous 
Australian peoples as lesser beings, and their land 
being classifed as terra nullius or ‘empty land’. This 
devaluing and dehumanising treatment of Indigenous 
Australian peoples led to the discriminatory 
experiences of reservations, loss of citizenship, stolen 
generations and numerous other indignities both small 
and large.
Groups such as the Jews and the Irish were also 
discriminated against, even when they lived in 
European countries or in Britain. Negative stereotypes 
were applied to the ‘national’ or ‘racial’ identities of 
these groups, regardless of how little these stereotypes 
actually resembled the individuals and their 
communities. This view of ‘them’ and ‘us’ helped to form 
national connections but it also led to racist actions 
which negatively impacted on the persecuted groups.
Another significant development of the industrial 
period was the emergence of the middle class as a 
significant and powerful group. Previously, there was 
an upper class and a lower class. The technological 
changes of the industrial period resulted in a 
professional class of people such as teachers, lawyers 
and doctors. This middle class became significant, 
dominating understandings of culture, national 
identity and literature.
Starter activity
Ask the students to consider how our society treats 
different groups; for example, children, teenagers, 
migrants, disabled people and older people. How are 
these groups seen and how are they treated?
Discuss the power of stereotypes and the impact they 
can have on the way people are treated.
Resource and Activity sheets
On the Activity sheet, ‘Social hierarchies’, students use 
a Venn diagram to identify similarities and differences 
between the social hierarchies of the Middle Ages and 
the industrial period. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Indigenous Australian people’, 
shows a primary source illustration of an Indigenous 
Australian family in the first years of European 
settlement. Students use the Activity sheet, ‘Source 
analysis’, to guide them through the process of 
analysing the illustration. They are encouraged to 
consider different features of the image and how they 
help with understanding the values of the person 
who drew the source, as well as providing a stronger 
understanding of the socio-historical context. Make 
sure the students understand that bias means that a 
persons shows a prejudice towards (likes or dislikes) a 
group of people.
The Activity sheet, ‘The Irish’, informs students about 
how the English viewed Irish people during this time. 
Students add the missing vowels to complete the 
information, then consider three primary sources. On 
the Activity sheet, ‘Stereotypes and beliefs’, students are 
guided through the process of analysing these three 
primary sources. 
Extension activities
Have students work in small groups to research another 
group persecuted during this time period; for example, 
Africans, Jews, women in Australia and/or Britain, or the 
Chinese in Australia.
Ask students to find quotes and images that show 
how society viewed these different groups. Discuss the 
values these attitudes show.
Objectives
• Gain an understanding of how different groups 
in society were seen and treated
• Consider the impact that certain differences 
could have on the experiences of people who 
lived at that time 
• Consider how the industrial period may have 
changed different groups

ACHIEVE!   History: The Industrial Revolution, 1750–1914
53
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Social problems
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution.
Background
In the industrial period, many people faced difficult 
decisions about how to survive. Working in the 
factories was not always possible, and some people 
were moved regularly between working and 
unemployment, depending on their employers. This 
left them in the difficult situation of needing other 
ways to pay their bills and feed their families. The 
poorest of the poor turned to the workhouses, which 
were the government-sanctioned form of poverty 
relief. People in the workhouses were treated badly: 
forced to work long hours on pointless tasks that 
taught them no skills, separated from their family 
members and given very little food. To avoid the 
workhouses, people turned to shady activities such 
as prostitution, baby farming (poor women were paid 
to look after other people’s children), renting out 
rooms and begging. Activities such as prostitution 
endangered their lives as they were often mistreated 
by men and even murdered like Jack the Ripper’s 
victims. 
Other people’s activities gradually became more 
criminal. For example, some people forced family 
members into prostitution and some baby farmers 
killed the babies in their care. Others turned to murder, 
theft and burglary. The consequences for these 
actions were extreme. Many people were executed 
or transported to Australia for their crimes. But not 
engaging in these activities could be almost as dire. 
They often faced the prospect of death every day. 
In the late 1800s, some people began questioning the 
way that poor people and criminals were treated and 
this led to more enlightened attitudes. Social reformers 
created groups for the protection of children (National 
Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, 
NSPCC) and the protection of animals (Royal Society for 
the Prevention of Cruelty to animals, RSPCA). They also 
began helping poor people by providing soup kitchens 
and working to get prostitutes off the streets.
Starter activity
What are the social problems in our society? Identify at 
least two contemporary social problems. 
Discuss the complexity of these problems and possible 
solutions for them. Make sure these solutions would 
improve our society.
Resource and Activity sheets
On the Resource sheet, ‘Baby farming’, students read 
two primary sources and one secondary source that 
provide information about the 19th century practice of 
baby farming. Students analyse these sources on the 
Activity sheet, ‘Primary and secondary sources’. They 
are encouraged to identify the differences between the 
types of sources and explain their value. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Social reformers’, looks at the lives of 
two key social reformers: Henry Mayhew and Josephine 
Butler. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Age of sexual consent’, outlines 
the way that social reformers brought about positive 
change for the protection of children. The Activity 
sheet, ‘Protecting girls’, consolidates the information on 
the Resource sheet.
Extension activities
With the class, brainstorm alternative solutions to baby 
farming for the mothers of illegitimate children during 
the Industrial Revolution. Solutions could include:
• 
 providing state-run or factory-run day care
• 
 fining fathers who did not contribute to their 
children’s upkeep
• 
 state-run orphanages
• 
 official adoption with government monitoring
• 
 group homes.
Have students choose one idea and compose a speech 
that supports their idea with clear explanations and the 
use of convincing evidence. 
Objectives
• Identify key social problems during the 
Industrial Revolution
• Understand the significance of these problems
• Learn about the methods people used in 
attempting to address these problems

59
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – New ideas
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic knowledge of the 
Industrial Revolution.
Background
The 1700s and 1800s were a highly significant 
period when many new ideas emerged, including 
republicanism, liberalism and secularism. Sometimes 
this period is described as the Enlightenment. 
Emerging ideas challenged the status quo and 
allowed for the development of even more new ideas. 
The scientific approach of Enlightenment thinkers 
introduced a new focus on empirical learning and 
thinking. This paved the way for Darwin’s theory of the 
evolution of the species and later, and less admirably, 
social Darwinism.
This period was also significant for its development 
of national and imperial identities. Many European 
countries valued themselves and their successes based 
on their racial or national qualities. The governments of 
these countries saw value in extending their empires 
by invading other countries, particularly in Asia, Africa 
and the Americas, and turning them into colonies. The 
colonies and their people were seen as lesser in value 
and treated accordingly.
As the industrial period continued, the plight of the 
poor working class became more apparent. Social 
philosophers such as Friedrich Engels and Karl Marx 
began challenging society by outlining the idea of a 
new ‘communist’ society that could arise in the future 
after the Industrial classes rebelled and overthrew the 
class-based ruling system. 
Starter activity
Compile a class mind map summarising the social 
situation during the Industrial Revolution: poor 
working conditions, long hours, mistreatment of 
children, beatings and disregard for the poor. 
Ask the students to imagine that they lived during that 
time. 
• 
 What ideas do they have about changing their 
world?
• 
 What would be a perfect world for poor people? 
• 
 What would be a perfect world for rich people?
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘New ideas and movements,’ asks 
students to match names with definitions for the key 
ideas and movements emerging during the 1700s 
and 1800s. Students then consider these ideas and 
movements and choose one historical person to 
research. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Communism’, informs students 
about the philosophers who developed the idea of 
communism and the key features of their ideology. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Darwinism and social Darwinism’, 
students discover the positives and negatives that 
resulted from Charles Darwin’s theory about the 
evolution of the species. 
The Activity sheets, ‘Imperialism’ and ‘Colonialism’, 
explore the situation in colonised countries ruled by 
empires. ‘Imperialism’ defines the term and focuses on 
the British colonisation of China. ‘Colonialism’ considers 
the individual impacts of imperialism on the people of 
colonial India. 
Extension activities
Have students choose one key idea or movement from 
this unit and construct a poster about it, using either 
ICT or poster paper. They should:
• 
 outline the features of the movement or idea
• 
 identify when it was important, and consider the 
time period and what else was happening in the 
world at this time
• 
 identify where it happened and why
• 
 identify key figures connected to it 
• 
 discuss why it was important.
Ideas and movements: Chartism, communism, 
Darwinism, social Darwinism, imperialism, nationalism, 
egalitarianism, suffragette movement
Objectives
• Understand the key ideas and movements 
during the industrial period
• Consider how issues like Imperialism can have 
positive effects for one country and negative 
effects for another country
• Identify individuals related to some key ideas 
and movements of the industrial period

Map of the British Empire
Britain had a large empire in the 1800s. It had conquered many countries including Canada, 
Australia, China, India, Cuba, Egypt and British Somaliland. These countries became colonies of 
the British Empire. The British often treated the local people in their colonies badly.
Factory owners in Britain bought raw products like sugar, cotton and wool very cheaply from 
the colonies. They took the raw products back to Britain and turned them into products like 
shirts and lollies.
Britain wasn’t the only country that was industrialised. France, Germany and Japan started 
building their own factories in the late 1800s.

Activity sheet – The Industrial Revolution in Britain
Causes of the Industrial Revolution
The Industrial Revolution started in the 1700s (18th century). It began in Britain and then in 
America, France, Germany and Japan. Many machines were invented and used in factories. 
New transport like trains and steamships made it easier for people and products to travel. 
+  1 Highlight the keywords (important words) in the table.
 2  In your workbook, compile a glossary of unfamiliar words and write definitions for them.
Theme
Cause: Explanation
Agriculture
•  Enclosure laws: The government forced people to fence in fields. Land 
was now owned by individuals, not villages.
•  Stock breeding: Farmers began to mate animals selectively to increase 
their quality.
•  Farm machinery: Jethro Tull’s seed drill made planting faster and easier.
Factories
•  Textile machines: People used new machines to make cloth more quickly.
•  Bank loans: After banks were invented, people could get loans to invest in 
factories, machines and land.
•  Government support: The government encouraged businesses to build 
more factories.
•  Unskilled labour in factories: Factory owners hired women and children 
as unskilled workers. It was cheaper than hiring men.
People 
•  People movement: There were not enough jobs in the country. People 
moved to the cities to find jobs in the factories.
•  Medicine: Improvements in medicine meant fewer people got sick or 
died. The population grew from 8 million in 1801 to 26 million in 1881.
Transport
•  Turnpike tolls: People paid tolls to use the roads. The toll money was used 
to improve the roads, which made travel easier.
•  Trains: Steam trains were invented in 1825. People and products could 
move around more easily.
•  Canals for transport: Canals were built in the 1760s so that boats could 
be used to move coal and steel. This was faster than using roads.

Textiles workers
The Industrial Revolution brought many new inventions. The textiles or clothing industry  
was one of the first industries to use machines.
A machine has taken my job.  
T he Master says the machine is 
faster and they don’t have to employ 
so many people. Why would they want 
me when they can hire some kid and 
pay them a quarter of the money?
Kevin T, aged 30 years, 
expert weaver.
I’ve got a job working on the 
machines because my family needs the 
money. It’s long hours and I don’t get 
paid the same as grown-ups. Sometimes 
I get beaten if I’m not fast enough 
or if I start to fall asleep.
James Hargreaves, aged 35 years, 
inventor of the spinning jenny.  
This machine spun thread faster 
so fewer workers were needed.
John Kay, aged 40 years, inventor of the flying shuttle. 
This machine allowed each weaver to make more cloth.
Mary D, aged 9 years, 
child labourer
I was attacked by textiles 
workers afraid of my Flying 
Shuttle invention putting them 
out of work. A friend helped 
me escape from nearly being 
killed by the textiles workers.
T he harassment was 
so bad from the 
textiles workers that 
I had to move towns.
I’m from West Yorkshire. 
T hey call me a Luddite 
because I don’t like the 
new machines. From 1811 
to 1816, textiles workers 
like me got into gangs. 
We broke into factories 
and smashed the machines 
to try and save our jobs.
Victor T, aged 30 years, 
textiles worker

Coal mining
+  Read the information and answer the questions below.
Coal mining became more important during the Industrial Revolution, because coal was 
a more efficient fuel than wood. Steam engines used coal for fuel. These engines powered 
machines in factories, trains and steamships.
Families often worked together in a colliery (coal mine). Fathers and sons cut or ‘hewed’ the 
coal from the stone. Mothers and daughters carried or ‘hurried’ the coal through the pit.
A load of coal weighed up to 150 kg. Sometimes it was so hot and dirty in the pits that miners 
worked naked. In 1842, the British government passed the Mines Act which banned boys under 
the age of ten and women and girls from working underground.
1 What is Betty’s job called? What did her job involve?
 
 
2  What does Betty mean by ‘the family way’? How would this affect her ability to work?
 
 
 
 
3  How do you think Betty’s story contributed to the introduction of the Mines Act in 1842?
 
 
 
 
Betty Harris, age 37 years, to the 1840 Royal Commission into mines
I was married at 23, and went into a colliery when I was married … I 
am a drawer, and work from 6 in the morning to 6 at night. Stop about an 
hour at noon to eat my dinner; have bread and butter for dinner; I get 
no drink … I worked at drawing when I was in the family way. I have a 
belt round my waist, and a chain passing between my legs, and I go on my 
hands and feet. T he road is very steep, and we have to hold by a rope; and 
when there is no rope, by anything we can catch hold of … My clothes are 
wet through almost all day long … the belt and chain is worse when we are 
in the family way. My feller (husband) has beaten me many a time for not 
being ready. I were not used to it at first, and he had little patience.

Transportation
Before the Industrial Revolution, most products were 
made and used locally. But after factories were built, 
business owners often got raw materials from the 
colonies because it was cheaper. They also sent their 
finished products further away to increase their profits. 
For transport, people could use either boats or horses 
and carts. This limited the distances they could travel 
and it was expensive. However, in the 1700s and 1800s 
transport changed.
Improvements in transport in the 1700s and 1800s
•  Road users paid turnpike tolls. The local authorities 
used this money to maintain and improve the roads so 
that people could travel faster.
•  From the mid-1700s, canals (inland waterways for 
boats) were built. This made it easier to get products 
onto boats and then around the country.
•  Railway tracks were laid, and horses were used to pull 
wagons along them. Now, heavy raw materials and products  
could be moved along regular routes; for example, from a coal mine to a port. 
+

21
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
This is a clipper, like the ones that brought many of the first 
Europeans to Australia. They were made of wood and the 
wind moved them swiftly across the water. They took 
two to four months to sail from Britain to Australia.
The poorest people travelled in steerage at the 
bottom of the ship. There was only one large 
room for all the steerage passengers. During 
storms, they had to stay in the dark because 
candles or lanterns might set the ship on 
fire. Water often leaked in through the sides of the ship 
so everything was wet. They slept in narrow wooden bunk beds  
and kept their possessions in large wooden trunks to keep them safe. 
Steamships like this were used in the 1890s and 1900s. 
They were powered by steam engines. At first, 
these ships weren’t much faster than clippers, 
but they were safer and more comfortable. 
Rich passengers travelled in cabins. There were 
restaurants and areas where passengers 
could read, play table tennis and 
hold concerts.
The poorest people travelled in 
steerage at the bottom of the ship. 
But steamships had more than one room in steerage. Each family had their own small cabin. 
Sometimes the cabins had a wash basin and a chest of drawers to help store their possessions. 
They could use lanterns or, later, electrical lights, even during storms.

Convicts and crime 
Crime rates increased during the industrial period because people moved from the country to 
the cities and could not find work. 
The prisons in Britain became overcrowded. They could no longer send convicts to America, 
so the government decided to transport them to Australia. From 1788 to1868, British criminals 
were often sent to Australia to serve their sentences. 
Crimes punished by transportation to Australia
* Being in the company of criminals – Life imprisonment
* Bigamy (married to two people at the same time) – 7 years
* Pickpocketing (stealing a small amount) – 7 years
* Vagrancy (being homeless) – 7 years
* T heft of a handkerchief – 7 years
* Murder – Life imprisonment

Indigenous Australian

Indigenous peoples have lived in Australia for thousands 
of years. Before 1788, there were many different groups 
with their own languages, laws and beliefs. These groups 
established their own territories. 
In 1788, the first British convicts were sent to Australia with 
the First Fleet. Australia was divided into two parts: the British 
colony of New South Wales in the east and the Dutch colony 
of New Holland in the west.
Over time, Australia was divided into colonies that had their 
own governments. In 1901, Australia became one federated 
country. The colonies became the states and territories we 
recognise today: Victoria, New South Wales, South Australia, 
Western Australia, Queensland, Tasmania Northern Territory 
(separated from South Australia in 1911) and the Australian 
Capital Territory (established in 1911).

British suffragettes
+ 
 Read the information and answer the questions below.
Suffrage means the right to vote. In Britain in the 
1700s and 1800s, only rich men who owned property 
were allowed to vote. 
In the late 1800s, many women started to protest. 
They wanted to vote and they wanted more rights. 
These women were called suffragettes. 
Many men and some women thought that 
suffragettes should not have the vote. They mocked 
these women in the newspapers by describing them 
as silly or masculine. Suffragettes were sentenced to 
prison for protesting. Many went on hunger strikes; 
the jailers would tie them down and push tubes 
down their throats to force-feed them.
During World War I, a lot of British suffragettes 
stopped protesting to support the war effort. Many 
historians believe this patriotism is why women over 
30 years were given the right to vote in 1918. In 1928, the voting age for women  
was reduced to 21 years, as it was for men. Finally, women had equal suffrage. 
1  How would you have protested if you were a suffragette? Explain why.
 
 
 
 
2  Write two questions you still have about this period in history. Use question words like 
who, what, where, when, how and why.
 
 
 
 
3  Choose one of your questions and research it using your textbook, the internet or your 
library. Answer the question in your workbook.

• Letter-writing campaigns 
• Protest marches 
• Signing petitions
•  Learning jujitsu so they could 
protect themselves
• Breaking windows
•  Standing on street corners and 
preaching to the crowds
• Chaining themselves to railings
• Hunger strikes in prison
•  Emily Davison ran in front of 
King George V’s horse at a 
horse race in 1913 and was 
killed.

Marriage and divorce laws
For many years, married couples found it almost impossible to legally separate unless they 
were incredibly rich and could convince the government to allow them to do so. In 1857, 
Britain finally allowed divorces for two causes: adultery committed by the wife and aggravated 
adultery committed by the husband. The colonies of Australia were allowed to form their own 
divorce laws.

Writing women
Women were expected to act in particular ways: be domestic, stay at home, let men make their 
decisions and above all to be mothers and wives, not doctors or lawyers. In the 1800s, some 
writers began exploring the idea of women being equal with men. 
English author Charlotte Bronte wrote Jane Eyre. 
This is a story about a poor governess who lived in 
England in 1847. Originally, Charlotte used the male 
pen-name Currer Bell because she was thought 
no-one would publish a book written by a woman.
Australian author Henrietta Dugdale was a 
suffragette, which means a woman who wants the 
right to vote. Her book A few hours in a far-off age 
written in 1883 explored the idea of an equal future.

Caroline Chisholm
My name is Caroline Chisholm. I was born in 1808 in England. From a 
very early age I cared about being a philanthropist. A philanthropist is 
someone who helps people who are poor or uncared for. I only married 
my husband Captain Archibald Chisholm because he allowed me to be a 
philanthropist and help others.
In 1838, my husband and I moved to Sydney, Australia. T here were 
many people who travelled to Australia but then had nowhere to go. 
I focused on helping poor immigrant girls. Many arrived with little money 
and there were not many respectable or safe places for them to stay. 
+

 2  Think of a strong woman you know who cares for people like Caroline Chisholm did.  
This could be a family member, friend, historical figure or celebrity. Explain why you 
admire them. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
With the help of Governor and Lady Gipps, I started 
a F emale Immigrants Home. We could house ninety-six 
women. We also had an employment agency to help the 
women find jobs so they could support themselves.
I supported families in moving to Australia and cared 
about the position of women and children when others 
did not. Later, I supported universal suf frage, the idea 
that every person deserves the right to vote and to be 
represented by their government.

The Poor Laws
+ Copy and complete the sentences in the right column in your workbook.
In Britain in the 1600s and 1700s there was no 
Centrelink to help unemployed or disabled people. 
Instead, they had the Poor Laws to look after 
people in the community who were struggling. 
1  Today we have ____ to help 
_____. 
2  In the 1600s and 1700s, they had 
_____ to help _____.
The Poor Laws meant that each church parish was 
responsible for looking after unemployed or sick 
people within its community. Richer people in the 
parish had to donate money to help the needy.
3  In the 1600s and 1700s, each 
church parish had to ____.
Before the Poor Laws, many poor people were 
punished by being put in stocks or whipped, just 
because they were poor. It didn’t matter if they had 
no choice about being unemployed.
4  The Poor Laws meant that poor 
people were no longer ____.
In 1834, the government made a new Poor Law to 
get poor people off the streets. They were put into 
places called workhouses. The people who set up 
the workhouses deliberately made them extremely 
harsh places to be. This meant that only the most 
desperate poor people would go there. 
5  Workhouses were introduced in 
____.
6  The people who set up the 
workhouses only wanted the 
most desperate poor people to 
go there because ____.
In the workhouses, families were separated. 
There were different spaces for men, women and 
children. They were given little food and had to 
work long hours on tasks that gave them no useful 
skills. They often wore prison-style uniforms and 
were locked away behind big walls. Some people 
described it as being like a prison for poor people.
7  The three worst things about 
workhouses were ____.

Resource sheet – Men
Society’s expectations
The Industrial Revolution was a time of significant change for men. Some men became 
powerful with the development of factories. But in many ways, the traditional ideas about men 
and masculinity were challenged by the new ideas and practices of the Industrial Revolution. 
Society’s expectations of men
Reality for men
• Be the breadwinner
•  Be the only worker outside the 
house 
• Support his family
Many lower class men were unemployed because 
their wages were too expensive, compared to 
women’s and children’s wages. 
Women and children often became family 
breadwinners.
•  Head of the household
•  In charge of everything that 
happens
• Make all the decisions
Many women were the family breadwinners. This 
gave them more decision-making power. 
The suffragette movement pushing for women to 
have the vote threatened the position of men as 
head of the household.
•  Handle all situations with strength, 
showing no emotion
Men were expected to show no emotion, even 
though they had feelings like everyone else. This 
made them feel distant from their families because 
they couldn’t be honest with them about the 
problems they had.
• Heterosexual
•  All serious and responsible men 
are married
There had always been homosexuals in society. 
But in the 1800s, social change led to a growing 
awareness of homosexuality which only increased 
as more men and women expressed their true 
preferences. Homosexuality was against the law in 
many countries at the time.
•  Physically strong
•  Always stronger then women 
and children
Many physically strong, lower class men were 
unemployed. Therefore, their physical strength was 
not so valuable. Many middle class men worked in 
businesses where they did little physical labour. This 
did not fit with society’s expectation that they be 
physically strong.

Chartists
The Chartist movement was a group of men, 
mostly working class, who wanted to change 
how the British government worked. But since 
they could not vote in elections, how could they 
change the government? Rich men who owned 
property could vote. They were usually from 
noble families. Poor men, women and children 
could not vote.
In 1838, the Chartists created a ‘People’s Charter’ 
to identify the rights they wanted. 
Rights from the People’s Charter
•  Full male suffrage – all males vote, 
whether they own property or not.
•  Secret ballot – people vote secretly so 
government ministers can’t mistreat 
people who didn’t vote for them.
•  Pay for parliamentarians, so poor people 
can afford to be parliamentarians too.
•  Equal-size electorates – one small district 
should not have more power than a 
large district.
•  Annual elections – people can change 
leaders each year if they aren’t looking 
after the interests of the country.
Resource sheet – Men
Most Chartists were working class people. They were unhappy  
about doing all the work, but not having a voice in how the country  
was governed. They signed petitions, organised strikes and held protest marches.
In the 1840s, the British government brought in soldiers to stop the movement. At least 
60 Chartist leaders were arrested and transported to Australia. Later, some of these men 
became involved in the Eureka Rebellion in 1854 in Ballarat, Australia, working for the same 
rights they fought for as Chartists.
Only responsible people like me should 
be able to vote. T he poor people do 
not have enough education to know 
what is best for our country. If they 
only worked hard enough to make 
money like I did then they would 
deserve to vote too. But they don’t.
It is not fair. I work hard my 
whole life and nobody ever listens 
to me. Politicians only think about 
themselves and their rich friends. 
T hey do not think about me and my 
family. Just because I am poor does 
not mean that I do not have ideas 
or needs.

Education
+  Cross out the incorrect word in each set of brackets.
Before the Industrial Revolution, only upper and middle class (children / child) went to 
school or were tutored. (Pour / Poor) children learned how to work from (there / their) 
parents or became apprentices to a master to learn a trade. Masters did not pay wages to 
apprentices because they were learning, but usually provided food and (housing / house).
In the 1830s, governments in Britain and Australia became concerned that children 
(were / where) becoming criminals because they were not (been / being) educated. 
They were also left unsupervised all day while their parents worked.
In Australia, governments established schools (too / to) educate children. Some religious 
groups like the Catholics and Anglicans also established schools. School wasn’t compulsory, 
so some parents kept (their / they’re) children at home when they needed them to work.
Students usually learned English, Arithmetic, Geography and 
History. Boys (were / we’re) sometimes taught Latin, while 
girls were usually taught sewing and knitting. Students often 
learned by repetition, to teach them obedience.
Children who did well at school could apply to be pupil teachers 
when they finished their schooling. They assisted for (two / to) 
years and (by / buy) the age of 15 they could be teachers.
In 1872, Victoria became the first Australian colony 
to make education free, secular and compulsory. This 
meant that children did not have to pay, no religion 
controlled what (were / was) studied, and all children 
had to attend. Society now (thought / taught) that it 
was more important for children to study than work.
Schooling became compulsory in Scotland in 
1872 and in Britain in 1880. Compulsory education 
reduced the number of child workers. Most children 
(know / now) began work when they were 12.
Every morning we repeat our 
times tables as a class. T he 
teacher says it helps us to learn 
the numbers. T hen we write 
the alphabet on our boards. 
It has to look exactly like the 
way the teacher writes it. 
If we forget our numbers or if 
our writing is not neat, we get 
hit to make us remember.

45
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Resource sheet – Children
Child labourers
Factory lives
In the industrial period, many people moved to the cities to work in factories. Factory wages 
were low. This meant that everyone in the family, including young children, often had to work 
to help the family survive. The conditions in factories were harsh. 
• Children could start working at the age of five years.
• The work was boring and repetitive.
• They worked long hours, sometimes 14 or 16 hours a day.
• Overseers beat children who did not work fast enough.
•  Children lost arms and legs or died if they got trapped in 
the machinery. 
Workhouses
Some orphans and poor people were kept in places called 
workhouses. The people there were often separated from 
their family members. They were given very little food 
and worked very hard. Friedrich Engels called workhouses 
‘Poor Law Bastilles’. This meant he thought they were prisons 
for the poor.
Parish apprentices
Church parishes were made up of people who lived in the 
same area, and were led by a priest. The parish had to look 
after the poor in their community. This included children 
who were orphans or half-orphans, which meant they had 
only one parent. The parish helped the children find jobs 
by sending them out as apprentices to be taught useful 
skills. The children were fed and clothed for their work, but 
rarely paid. The masters took them as a charitable act. If the 
masters refused to take the children, they had to pay the 
parish a fine. 
Elizabeth Bentley began 
work at a flax mill when she 
was 6 years old. On busy 
days, she worked from 5 am 
to 9 pm. That’s 16 hours, 
with only a 40 minute break 
for lunch.
One boy, George Orange from Leeds, was taken and returned almost weekly. 
This made his parish a good amount of money through fines.
Friedrich Engels was a rich 
German. His father owned 
factories in England, but he 
didn’t want to be a factory 
owner. Instead, he wrote 
about the experiences of 
the working class.

Baby farming
Source 1
Baby farming became more frequent during the Industrial Revolution. 
When single women or widows became pregnant, they often struggled 
to both look after a child and keep a job to support them. Many women 
turned to ‘baby farmers’ to care for their children. Baby farmers were often 
married women or widows who took in and looked after babies for money. 
The problems began when mothers stopped paying for their children’s 
support or when the baby farmers became greedy. Many children in the 
care of baby farmers died of malnutrition or neglect. Some were murdered.
Baby farmers accused of murdering babies include Amelia Sach and 
Annie Walters in England, Minnie Dean in New Zealand, and Frances Knorr 
and John and Sarah Jane Makin in Australia.
Rachel Towns, Achieve! History – The Industrial Revolution, Clayton, 
Blake Education, 2017, Australia.
Source 2

•  They were made at the time being 
studied and show something about 
the world at that time. 
•  They usually focus on specific events or 
issues.
For example, a diary written in 1944 about 
World War II is a primary source.

Criminal Amendment Act of 1885
The age of consent is when someone can legally engage in sexual activity. 
In Britain, the age of consent had been 12 years since the 
Westminster statutes of 1275. Twelve years was also the age you 
could get married. In the Middle Ages, people married young 
as they also often died young. However, as people began 
to live longer they began to see 12 year olds as children 
rather than potential marriage partners.
Social reformers including William Stead (editor of 
the Pall Mall Gazette), Bramwell Booth (Salvation 
Army) and Josephine Butler (a protector of 
women) became concerned about what they 
called the ‘white slave trade’. This referred to 
the practice of selling young girls to brothels 
as prostitutes. 
In 1883, William Stead wrote a series of 
articles called The Maiden Tribute of Modern 
Babylon. He described the terrible situations 
experienced by young women living in poverty, especially in London. Finally, he drew attention 
to the white slave trade by describing how easy it was for him to purchase a girl aged 13 years. 
He pretended that he worked for a French brothel, and approached a woman named Rebecca 
Jarrett who specialised in finding girls for brothels. Rebecca arranged for William to purchase 
Eliza Armstrong from her mother for five pounds. After demonstrating how easy it was to buy 
young girls for brothels, Bramwell Booth arranged for Eliza to move in with a Salvationist family.
William’s articles about purchasing Eliza resulted in a court case where he faced changes for 
buying a girl. He was imprisoned for three months. The publicity surrounding the articles, 
court case and prison sentence encouraged the government to change the age of consent 
from 12 years to 16 years with the Criminal Amendment Act of 1885.

Imperialism
+  1 Write each underlined word beside the correct definition below.
European countries often had great military strength. They had new weapons, such as guns 
and cannons, which they used to overpower other countries. Britain became one of the biggest 
empires in the world in the 1800s. They controlled large parts of Asia, Africa, Canada, Australia 
and many other key regions. The countries ruled by the British were called colonies. These 
colonies had little say in how they were ruled. They did not have the weapons of the British and 
so they had no hope of successfully fighting back. 
Britain won two wars in China in the 1800s: the First Opium War in 1842 and the Second Opium 
War in 1858. In both wars they gained more control over China. This was valuable because they 
wanted tea, silk, spices and other luxury products that only came from China. 
In many of the British colonies, particularly in Asia and Africa, local people were encouraged 
to learn English. Often, English became the official language of the colony. Local people who 
became Anglophiles and adopted British practices were often treated better than those who 
did not. But they were still not treated as well as British people.

My name is Rhett. I am an Anglo-Indian. My father, Geof frey, 
is a British soldier and my mother, T hirumangai, is Indian. It was 
quite normal for British men to marry Indian women because 
there were so few British women in India. Or at least there 
weren’t many before the 1850s. 
Anglo-Indians, like me, were born to Indian and British parents. 
We often have lighter skin, speak English and wear English 
clothes. Being Anglo-Indian is useful as the British, who rule over 
India, give more jobs to Anglo-Indians than other Indians. We 
aren’t treated as well as the British, which is a pity – I see 
myself as more British than Indian.
My name is Ishmeet. I want to be an engineer when I 
grow up. My father and mother tell me to stop dreaming 
such silly dreams. T hey tell me to look at my face in the 
river and I will know what I will really become. It hurts 
me when they say such things, but I know it to be true. 
I am an Indian, my skin is darker than the skin of the 
British people who rule over us. When they look at me they 
do not see how smart I am, how many languages I can 
speak or the dreams I have. All they see is my skin. All the 
good jobs go to the British first, the Anglo-Indians second 
and then all other Indians last. I probably can’t ever be 
an engineer. But I still dream about it all the same.

Achieve!   History – World War I – Book 1
5
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Alliances
Background
World War I was triggered by a climate of fear in 
Europe. Alliances between countries were a major 
cause of World War I and divided Europe into two 
groups – the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente. It is 
important that students understand why alliances are 
created and their impact on other countries in order to 
understand the climate of insecurity and uncertainty 
that these generated, and which caused countries 
across Europe to go to war. 
Starter activity
Discuss the basic concepts described in the 
background material with students. Ask them what 
they know about Europe and World War I. Introduce 
them to the terms ‘alliance’ and ‘Europe’. Help students 
to make a personal connection to the concept of 
alliances by holding a class discussion using these 
starter questions:  
• What would you do if you saw a fight? 
• Would you help your best friend if they got in a 
fight? Why/why not?  
• Is the enemy of your enemy your friend? Why/why 
not?
Resource and Activity sheets
The first Activity sheet, ‘Personal experience of 
alliances’, helps students to identify personal 
connections to the concept of alliances, which were 
a major cause of World War I. Encourage students 
to make connections to their own lives, referencing 
relevant literature covered in class or recent media 
stories featuring key alliances. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Alliances causing conflict’, 
introduces students to the two alliances of World War I  
and how conflict arose between them. The text also 
examines how Australia would be affected if the Triple 
Entente went to war.  
The Activity sheet, ‘Mapping the alliance divide’, 
examines the geographical divide between the 
countries in the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente. 
Discuss the distance between the countries and how 
this may have affected their choice of alliance. Draw 
students’ attention to the countries not in an alliance 
and discuss why these countries may have chosen to 
stay neutral. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘The need for alliances’, students 
further explore the alliances and read a case study of 
the Triple Entente before answering literal, inferential 
and evaluative questions. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Summarising alliances’, asks 
students to summarise the content and concepts they 
have learnt. Discuss the importance of summarising 
when learning new information, and demonstrate how 
to identify and use key words in the text. 
Extension ideas
Many deals and alliances were made between 
countries in Europe from 1879 to 1914, ultimately 
leading to the Triple Alliance and Triple Entente. 
Students could research these alliances and create a 
timeline showing the deals formed. This timeline could 
form the basis of a class discussion. 
Examples of alliances to research:
• Dual Alliance (1879)
• Austro-Serbian Alliance (1881)
• The Triple Alliance (1882)
• The Franco-Russian Alliance (1894)
• The Entente Cordiale (1904)
• The Triple Entente (1907) 
The following websites could be helpful:
• www.bbc.co.uk/history/worldwars/wwone 
• www.greatwar.co.uk/research/ww1-research-index.
htm
• www.awm.gov.au
Objectives
• To understand the causes of World War I 
• To learn some key terms and concepts 
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities. 
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

Achieve!   History – World War I – Book 1
11
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Militarism
Background
World War I was triggered by the rise of militarism  
in Europe. Countries were building up their armies, 
navies and air forces in competition with each other,  
in preparation for an inevitable war in Europe. 
Starter activity
Ask students what they know about the military. 
Introduce them to images and vocabulary associated 
with the military, such as guns, soldiers and the army. 
Students should be exposed to images from modern-
day wars and 1914-era warfare. Hold a class discussion 
about developments and features of the military 
including the nature of warfare in 1914 compared  
to today.  
Resource and Activity sheets
The first Activity sheet, ‘Defining militarism’, provides 
students with an understanding of language structure 
and the use of ‘ism’ to change a noun to refer to an 
attitude or belief. This helps students distinguish 
between the military and the idea of militarism. 
Students use synonyms to create their own definition 
of militarism.  
The Resource sheet, ‘The need for militarism’, explains 
why countries adopted militarism. Through a case 
study, students identify the competition between 
countries to increase their military presence.
The Resource sheet, ‘Interviewing the British Empire’, 
demonstrates how to ask questions in order to gain 
more information about a topic or person. It models 
the 5W and 1H question structure, using an engaging 
example to encourage class discussion.  
In the Activity sheet, ‘Interviewing the German Empire’, 
students ask their own 5W and 1H questions about 
Germany’s military strategy in the lead-up to World 
War I. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Summarising militarism’, helps 
students summarise their knowledge of militarism by 
responding to True or False questions about the topic. 
Extension ideas
Students could brainstorm what the environment of 
militarism in early twentieth-century Europe would 
have been like compared to modern Australian 
military operations. For example, resources were 
directed to building arms and munitions rather than 
spending this money on addressing social issues. 
Students could then explore one specific difference 
between military practices in 1914 and today. 
Questions students could consider include:
• Does this practice still happen in areas of the world 
today?
• Why do some countries continue to support 
militarism?
• Would militarism work in modern Australia? Would 
modern Australian citizens vote for militarism 
before addressing social issues?
Objectives
• To understand the causes of World War I 
• To learn some key terms and concepts 
• To identify different kinds of questions about 
the past 
Prior knowledge
Students should understand what militarism is 
and how an arms race can create the conditions 
for war.

Achieve!   History – World War I – Book 1
17
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Nationalism
Background
World War I was fought for many years because 
of growing nationalism in Europe. Nationalism 
encouraged citizens to sacrifice their lifestyles and 
safety in order to work for, fight for and defend their 
country. It is important that students understand how 
nationalism benefited European leaders and how this 
was generated in order to comprehend the strong 
nationalism that drove nations to compete against 
each other rather than working together. 
Starter activity
Discuss nationalism with students. Introduce them to 
the idea of having loyalty to a sports club, their family 
or friends. Highlight how loyalties can both unite and 
divide people. 
To demonstrate this, first unite the class by explaining 
that they all go to the same school, then divide up 
the students according to their sporting loyalties or 
the areas in which they live. This physically shows the 
students how their loyalties have the potential to unite 
or divide them. 
Resource and Activity sheets
In the Activity sheet, ‘Defining nationalism’, students 
write their own definition of nationalism. As an 
extension, students could write these definitions 
without the scaffolding support. Before commencing 
the activity, remind students what antonyms and 
synonyms are. 
The second Activity sheet, ‘Why promote nationalism?’, 
explores the advantages that nationalism provides to 
a nation’s leaders. Students illustrate each advantage 
before matching them with an explanation of the 
benefit to leaders.
The Activity sheet, ‘How to create nationalism’, explains 
how a country’s national symbols are used to promote 
nationalism, using national symbols of Australia and 
Great Britain as examples. Extend the activity by 
playing Australian national songs or showing physical 
examples of Australian national symbols for students 
to interact with. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘Living with nationalism’, 
students are encouraged to think about the personal 
experiences of people who lived through World War I. 
Students describe what living with nationalism would 
look like, feel like and sound like. As an extension, 
students could use these words to write a letter 
describing these experiences to a friend. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Summarising alliances’, gives 
students practice at summarising what they have 
learned about nationalism. They are shown how bullet 
points can be used to briefly summarise information in 
point form, making it easier to read.  
Extension ideas
Students could write a diary entry from the point of 
view of a citizen living in one of the countries that 
fought in World War I. They could research the allies 
and enemies of that country and identify the citizen’s 
contribution to the nation, such as undertaking food 
rationing, working in a factory, signing up for the army 
reserves, etc. 
Possible questions to explore include:
• What sacrifices are you making for your country?
• Why are you making these sacrifices?
• How do you feel towards your country’s allies?
• How do you feel towards your country’s enemies?
• What would you do if your country declared war on 
its enemies?
After writing their diary entries students could also 
conduct a role-play as their adopted citizens. 
Objectives
• To understand the causes of World War I 
• To learn key terms and concepts 
• To explore different forms of communication
Prior knowledge
Students would benefit from studying militarism 
in Unit 2 before undertaking this unit in order to 
understand the militaristic context that drives 
people to fight for their country.

Achieve!   History – World War I – Book 1
23
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Imperialism
Background
The lead-up to World War I saw many countries take 
over other nations in order to build an empire.  
This gave them power all over the world. It is 
important that students understand how imperialism 
allows countries to dominate others, and how this 
caused colonies such as Australia to be drawn into a 
war that was primarily fought in Europe. 
Starter activity
Discuss the geography of Europe and the world in 
1914. Ask students to choose different empires and 
colour a map to show the areas of land that those 
empires controlled. Ask students how they think those 
areas of land were taken over and why. 
Examples of empires in 1914 include:
• the British Empire
• the German Empire
• the Ottoman Empire
• the Austro-Hungarian Empire. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The first Activity sheet, ‘Defining imperialism’, provides 
students with vocabulary support to describe 
imperialism. Students should first find synonyms 
for the original words before looking them up in a 
dictionary. 
The Resource sheet, ‘How to build an empire’, explores 
the advantages of having a strong empire. Have 
students explore Australia as an example, encouraging 
them to debate whether Australia needed to fight in 
World War I and to question why it did so.
The Activity sheet, ‘Europe’s empires’, tests students’ 
knowledge of imperialism by asking questions about 
the topic.
The Activity sheet, ‘How to remember the causes of 
World War I’, enables students to summarise the four 
causes they have learnt about so far by associating 
each cause with a visual. Ask students to explain the 
relevance of the images to each cause and why the 
images have been chosen. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘Answering questions about 
the MAIN causes’, students write questions they 
have about the MAIN causes of World War I using 
the 5W and 1H structure. They then swap questions 
with another student and try to answer their peer’s 
questions. Students can access additional materials to 
answer these questions if required. 
Extension ideas
• Students could apply different summarising 
techniques (bullet points, finding key words, etc) to 
the different passages in the unit.
• Students could enhance the information by 
providing synonyms to replace the original words 
used. 
• Students could write a news article predicting what 
may have happened to each of the empires after 
the war.
Objectives
• To understand the causes of World War I 
• To learn key terms and concepts
• To compose effective questions about the past
Prior knowledge
As many activities refer to militarism concepts, it 
would be useful for students to have completed 
the Militarism unit before completing this unit.

Achieve!   History – World War I – Book 1
29
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Explaining the causes of 
World War I 
Background
Students will be aware of the causes of World War I  
from their study of Units 1–4. This unit will help 
students express their knowledge by planning and 
writing an essay about the causes of World War I. It 
is important that students are able to express their 
knowledge in writing, as this will be a requirement 
of students studying history at a senior level. 
Students also need to be able to sequence events 
chronologically on a timeline in order to better 
understand the chain of events that led to World War I. 
Starter activity
Introduce the subject of essay writing. Have students 
move into small groups, and appoint a scribe for each 
group. Give students some questions about essays 
for them to discuss, then have each group share their 
responses with the class. 
Questions could include:
• What makes a good essay? 
• What makes a good history essay? 
• What do you need to add to a history essay which 
would make it different to an English essay? 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Constructing essays’, poses 
questions to ensure that students fully understand 
set essay questions. A connection is drawn between 
essay construction and house construction in order to 
help students see essay construction as an achievable 
process, rather than a formal task. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Essay planning’, helps students to 
plan their essays by answering questions about each 
set paragraph. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Writing paragraphs’, helps students 
develop their bullet points into full sentences. As an 
extension, students could then use their full sentences 
to write a complete essay. 
In the Resource sheet, ‘Mapping events in a timeline’, 
students observe two examples of timelines, 
demonstrating the rules of how timelines work. 
The Activity sheet, ‘World War I trigger timeline’, 
gives students the opportunity to put the timeline 
rules into action. Students view the events leading 
up to World War I that triggered the war. Make sure 
students understand how the MAIN causes created the 
environment for war. 
Extension ideas
• Working as individuals or in small groups or pairs, 
students could plan and write other essays about 
the causes of the war. For example: What was the 
most important cause of World War I? Was World 
War I avoidable?
Objectives
• To understand the causes of World War I 
• To learn key terms and concepts
• To learn how to use different forms of 
communication
• To learn how to use chronological sequencing 
Prior knowledge
Students need to have prior knowledge of the 
causes of World War I (see Units 1–4). It would also 
be helpful for students to have completed the 
summarising activities in each of these units.

Achieve!   History – World War I – Book 1
35
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Triggers 
Background
While the MAIN (militarism, alliances, imperialism 
and nationalism) causes of World War I created the 
conditions for war, a spark or trigger was needed 
to start it. This unit looks at that trigger – the 
assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. This 
completes the overview of the causes of World War I 
and helps students understand how the trigger led to 
war, which was inevitable given the climate in Europe 
at the time. 
Starter activity
Have students predict what will trigger World War I by 
holding a class discussion. Questions you could ask 
include:
• How likely is the war?
• Are militarism, alliances, imperialism and 
nationalism enough to start the war?
• Who will start the war?
Encourage students to consider the idea of a trigger 
– something to start the war Europe had been 
conditioned to expect. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The first Activity sheet, ‘Language of triggers’, 
demonstrates language associated with triggers so 
that students can understand how World War I started. 
The Resource sheet, ‘The assassination of Archduke 
Franz Ferdinand’, gives students the background on 
the assassination that triggered the outbreak of war. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Crime scene report’, helps students 
identify key facts about the assassination in order to 
understand its significance. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Viewpoints of World War I (1)’, 
encourages students to consider the viewpoints of 
both sides. The Activity sheet, ‘Viewpoints of World  
War I (2)’, then encourages students to identify 
similarities and differences between the two sides 
and their role in starting the war. Students complete a 
Venn diagram using the information from the previous 
Activity sheet. They then articulate this information in 
full sentences using the sentence starters provided. 
Extension ideas
• Having compared the viewpoints of both sides 
in the lead-up to World War I, students could 
now adopt one of these viewpoints and write a 
persuasive essay or speech to convince others that 
their side is right. 
• Students could participate in a class debate, arguing 
that their chosen side was justified in engaging in 
World War I. 
Objectives
• To understand the causes of  World War I 
• To understand different perspectives
Prior knowledge
Students should be familiar with European 
geography and imperialism in order to 
understand the motivations behind the 
assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand.

Achieve!   History – World War I – Book 1
41
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Australia joins the war 
Background
World War I occurred due to the strength of alliances 
across Europe. Australia’s alliance with Britain meant 
that it also became involved. Viewpoints on Australia’s 
involvement in World War I differ. This unit helps 
students to identify and analyse these perspectives. 
Starter activity
Remind students about the Triple Alliance and the 
Triple Entente. Ask students how these alliances could 
lead to World War I, and encourage them to consider 
how war could be declared in practice. Students could 
consider the following questions:
• Who declares a war?
• Does being part of an alliance force you to join a 
war?
• Who declares a war first? 
Discuss Australia’s links to Britain and its consequent 
interest in the events of World War I despite its 
distance from Europe. 
Resource and Activity sheets
In the first Activity sheet, ‘Mapping the declaration of 
war’, students place declarations of war into the order 
in which they occurred. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Should Australia get involved?’, 
offers students an insight into the reasons Australia 
joined the fighting. Make sure students understand 
each reason before they progress to the next Activity 
sheet. 
The second Activity sheet, ‘Analysing viewpoints’, 
encourages students to analyse different viewpoints, 
articulating the strengths and weaknesses of each. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘Arguing a viewpoint’, students 
present their view of Australia’s role in World War I as a 
structured persuasive argument. This should include  
a topic sentence, three reasons for their viewpoint and 
a conclusion. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Different perspectives’, encourages 
students to consider the feelings of Australians from 
different backgrounds regarding Australia’s role in 
World War I.
Extension ideas
• Students could adopt the profile of a particular 
country and explain why they went to war, either 
by giving an oral presentation or writing a journal 
entry from the perspective of that country’s leader. 
Objectives
• To  understand different perspectives
• To investigate the different attitudes towards 
World War I in Australia
Prior knowledge
Students should be familiar with the alliances  
that were created, in order to help them 
understand why Australia needed to support 
Britain in World War I.

Achieve!   History – World War I – Book 1
47
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Recruiting an army
Background
When Australia declared its support for Britain in World 
War I, it needed to recruit soldiers to join the fight. 
While there were age, height and fitness restrictions 
for soldiers joining the army in 1914, these were 
soon relaxed as the death toll rose and the number 
of men enlisting declined. The idea of conscription 
was introduced as a way of raising army numbers, 
and the issue was voted on by the Australian public 
in 1915 and 1917. While both referendums failed, the 
conscription debate divided Australian society. 
Starter activity
Hold a class discussion about the reasons someone 
might choose to join the army. Ask students to 
consider the following questions, and write a personal 
response.
• Would you join the army?
• Would you kill for your country?
• Would you die for your country?
Students should review their response at the end of 
the unit to see if their opinion has changed once they 
have a better understanding of recruitment.  
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Who joins the war?’, informs 
students of the numbers of Australians who joined 
World War I. Students then analyse the extent of the 
initial Australian war effort. 
The second Activity sheet, ‘Recruitment 
advertisements (1)’, provides an example of a 
recruitment advertisement that employs the strategy 
of using a well-known soldier to encourage sportsmen 
to join the Australian army. The poster depicts 
Lieutenant Albert Jacka, VC, the first Australian to 
win the Victorian Cross during World War I. Students 
examine the use of propaganda by answering literal, 
inferential and evaluative questions about the 
advertisement. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Recruitment advertisements (2)’, 
continues the analysis of recruitment advertisements, 
focusing on the negative links drawn between the 
prospect of losing the war and having Germany 
dominate the world. Literal, inferential and evaluative 
questions build on the previous activity, enabling 
students to analyse and understand propaganda. 
The Resource sheet, ‘The conscription debate (1)’, 
introduces the idea of conscription and explains how 
the practice was almost introduced in Australia during 
World War I. Students analyse the issue in the Activity 
sheet, ‘The conscription debate (2)’, exploring reasons 
for and against conscription before forming their own 
opinion and constructing an argument to express this.
Extension ideas	
• Students could create their own World War I 
Australian recruitment advertisement. This should 
appeal to eligible men and tap into their emotions 
in order to persuade them to enlist.
• Students could research Lieutenant Albert Jacka, VC, 
and create a poster presenting information about 
his career and achievements.
Objectives
• To understand the use of propaganda
• To identify the reasons why men enlisted
• To use different communication forms 
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of the 
causes of World War I and the reasons behind 
Australia’s involvement. This will help them to 
understand why Australians were recruited for 
World War I.

Achieve!   History – World War I – Book 1
53
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Propaganda
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete this 
unit. 
Background
Nations used propaganda to win the hearts and 
minds of the people, convincing them of the benefits 
of war. This meant people were willing to serve in the 
armies and make sacrifices for the war effort. The use 
of propaganda in World War I was crucial in enabling 
countries to sustain contributions to the war effort. 
Starter activity
Ask students to persuade you to not give homework 
to the class. After hearing their arguments, ask 
students to consider whether they were balanced. 
Encourage them to consider how removing a 
balanced perspective increases the persuasiveness of 
the viewpoint being presented. Get students thinking 
about modern examples of propaganda, such as 
product advertisements or political propaganda 
during election campaigns. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The first Activity sheet, ‘Defining propaganda’, 
introduces students to the term ‘propaganda’ and 
addresses the importance of its use in World War I. 
The second Activity sheet, ‘Sources of propaganda’, 
introduces primary and secondary sources, linking 
them to sources of propaganda, both from World  
War I and the material that was written about it after 
the event. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Evaluation of propaganda: Primary 
sources’, asks students to evaluate primary sources, 
identifying the origin, purpose and context of each 
source.
The Activity sheet, ‘Evaluation of propaganda: 
Secondary sources’, asks students to evaluate 
secondary sources , again identifying the origin, 
purpose and context of each. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Using propaganda as evidence’, 
asks students to present their perspective on an issue, 
using primary and secondary sources to support their 
argument. 
Extension ideas
• After completing the Activity sheet, ‘Using 
propaganda as evidence’, students could write 
their opinion as an essay, using full sentences and 
paragraphs. 
• To further develop their public speaking skills, 
students could then give an oral presentation 
to the class, expressing their point of view and 
explaining how the source supports it. Students 
could use digital technology such as PowerPoint or 
Prezi, if available. 
Objectives
• To understand the use of propaganda
• To understand primary and secondary sources
• To process and blend information from a range 
of sources as evidence for an argument
