Achieve!   History – World War I – Book 1
59
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – The creation of the Anzacs
Background
The Anzac legend was born from Australia’s 
experiences in World War I. The term Anzac originally 
stood for Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, but 
by 1917 it referenced the men who fought at Gallipoli 
in World War I. Although it has since been used to 
describe all Australians killed in battle, it was during 
World War I that the courage, mateship and sacrifice of 
the Anzac legend was created. This is why we celebrate 
those qualities demonstrated by soldiers at Gallipoli 
each year on 25 April at dawn – the time and date of 
the Gallipoli landing. This unit teaches students about 
the men behind the Anzac legend. 
Starter activity
Ask students where they have seen the word Anzac 
before. Show students Gallipoli on a map from 1914 
and on a map from the present day. Explain that in 
1914 Gallipoli was part of the Ottoman Empire, which 
had an alliance with Germany. This will clarify why the 
Anzacs fought in this region in World War I. 
Introduce the topic of Anzac Day, which is observed 
on 25 April every year in Australia, and ask students to 
describe what they see, do and think about on the day. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The first Resource sheet, ‘Biographies of Anzacs (1)’, 
outlines the background of Australian soldiers in World 
War I, helping students understand what motivated 
them to fight in the war. A biography of a soldier who 
fought in World War I is also provided.
The second Resource sheet, ‘Biographies of Anzacs (2)’, 
offers further insight into different perspectives of the 
many Australians involved in World War I. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Biographies of Anzacs – Analysis’, 
asks students to investigate and analyse the individual 
perspectives of Australian soldiers. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘Biographies of Anzacs – 
Comparison’, students choose two of the four 
viewpoints presented in the Resource sheets, 
then complete a Venn diagram to compare the 
perspectives. Students then articulate the similarities 
and differences in full sentences, using information 
from the Venn diagram. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Where Australians fought in World 
War I’, outlines where Australians were stationed so 
students get a sense of how far the soldiers were from 
home, and how this affected their perspective of the 
fighting. 
Extension ideas
Having mapped the places where Australians fought 
in World War I, students could explore the extent of the 
fighting by shading the map according to colonial ties, 
assigning a colour to each empire. 
Additionally students could also investigate one of 
the countries Australians fought in. The following 
questions could form the basis of their investigation:
• What climate (weather) do these countries have? 
• Look at the country on a world map. How far away 
from Australia is it? 
• How did Australian soldiers travel to the country?
• How long did it take them to get there?
• How would an Australian soldier feel after this 
journey?
• Would you feel well-rested and ready to fight?
Objectives
• To investigate and understand the Anzac 
tradition
• To understand different perspectives
• To identify parts of the world that were 
involved in, or affected by, World War I 
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that the Australian 
army fought in World War I and understand why 
Australia joined the war.

may have alliances in your own life, such as the friendships you have at school, or your 
teammates on a sports team. Other kinds of alliances include treaties between countries.

Resource sheet – Alliances
Alliances causing conflict 
How this affected Australia
Australia was aligned with Britain as a member of the British Commonwealth.  
If Britain was to go to war, Australia was likely to become involved. Australian soldiers 
would fight alongside the Triple Entente soldiers. Citizens of Triple Alliance countries 
living in Australia would also be considered enemies of Australia once Australia joined 
the fighting. 
World War I (1914–1918) was the first war to involve countries in all areas of the world. 
Millions of people died in the conflict. 
World War I was a struggle between Europe’s great powers. What started as a fight 
between two countries quickly escalated into full-scale war as other countries joined the 
fighting to defend their allies. On one side was the Triple Alliance (also known as the 
Central Powers because they were in the centre of Europe). This alliance was formed 
between Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy and the Ottoman Empire (later called Turkey). 
On the other side was the Triple Entente (French for Allied Powers). This was an alliance 
between the British Empire, France and Russia (America also joined them later in the fight).

Activity sheet – Alliances
The need for alliances 
Alliances are agreements made between countries to help each other. This means that 
the enemy of your friend becomes your enemy, too. For example, Britain and France were 
allies, so they were united against each other’s enemies. 
An alliance can:
• provide protection against threats and invasions
• make a country look more powerful
• make other countries (who are not part of the alliance) feel vulnerable and threatened
• mean a country has to join in the fighting if its ally declares war against another country.
The Triple Entente 
Since 1879 Germany had been forming alliances with countries across Europe. Britain, 
France and Russia formed the Triple Entente in 1907 to protect themselves against the 
increasing power of Germany. As a result of this alliance, an enemy of one country would 
also become an enemy of the other countries, and if one country declared war, then all 
countries would go to war.
+ 
Use the information about alliances above to answer these questions. 
1	 What are two people in an alliance called?
	
	
	
	
2	 Why do countries form alliances? 
	
	
	
	
3	 How would you feel if your neighbours were forming secret alliances?
	
	
	
	
4	 How could alliances trigger a war?

Interviewing the British Empire 
When many countries are all ruled and controlled by one more-powerful country, this 
is called an empire. Countries under the control of an empire are called colonies. Many 
countries in Europe had empires. By 1914, the British Empire was the largest empire in the 
world, ruling over a quarter of the land on Earth. It controlled so much of the world that 
people would say, ‘the sun never sets on the British Empire’. As the world turned, the sun 
would always be shining on a country that was part of the British Empire. Countries under 
British control included India and Australia. 
We ask questions to find out more information about something. The questions below will 
help you explore how the size of the British Empire contributed to the outbreak of World 
War I. The questions follow the 5W and 1H structure. 
The 5Ws and 1H are:

• How?

The German Empire was made up of other countries (colonies) controlled by Germany. 
Germany expanded its empire in the lead-up to World War I, in an attempt to rival Great 
Britain, who had the largest empire. Although it wasn’t as large as the British Empire, by 1913 
the German Empire included areas which are today part of France, Russia and Poland.

Activity sheet – Nationalism 
Why promote nationalism?
Nationalism means that people are willing to support their country and its rulers or 
government. This means that the leader of the country will have:
• people who are willing to be soldiers in their army
• workers to make guns in their arms factories
• more freedom to make unpopular decisions (people will be willing to make sacrifices)
• increased national security (more people will want to defend their country)
• support for sacrifices such as rationing and conscription. 
+

How to create nationalism 
Nationalism can be developed through the use of signs or symbols. To make a country 
seem more important to its people, the leaders of a country will use symbols and icons. 
They promote these symbols so that people see them often and become attached to 
them. This helps develop loyalty and passion. 
+
